title: DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
content_c:
DUP blocks Michelle O'Neill's engagements over Drumcree
- Published
Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill has been blocked by the DUP from attending an economic summit involving Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The Sinn Féin vice-president and Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly were both invited to attend the National Economic Council in Glasgow on Friday with other devolved leaders.
The DUP leader Gavin Robinson confirmed that his party colleague Little-Pengelly will not participate in joint engagements with O'Neill and permission will not be granted for the first minister to operate on a solo basis.
The move follows unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests which prevented a contentious Orange Order march in Portadown from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
A meeting of the party's ruling officer committee was held earlier on Thursday.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson said the first minister's "arrogance will have consequences", but O'Neill accused the party of being "reckless and irresponsible".
"Her complaints today that she's frustrated from engaging with the British Prime Minister within the sovereign United Kingdom will so be it because her law breaking must have consequences," Robinson said.
O'Neill said the DUP leader's comments were "arrogant and supremacist" adding that the DUP "is consumed with their own internal leadership troubles and divisions".
She said she would be at the Assembly on Monday with her party colleagues to "keep showing up every day for people".
Earlier she described the move to block the meeting with the prime minister as "reckless and irresponsible" and meant people in Northern Ireland "will not be represented".
"This is a reactive stunt, driven by the DUP's own internal pressures and electoral problems," she said in a statement posted online.
The prime minister revived the National Economic Council over the summer to encourage greater collaboration between the nations and regions.
Earlier Little-Pengelly said the concerns arising from O'Neill's conduct and the "anger and hurt felt by many people across Northern Ireland, cannot simply be ignored or minimised".
She said the decision comes after stopping a separate planned engagement with the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly.
"I have requested a separate meeting with the Prime Minister to ensure Northern Ireland's interests, including the urgent budgetary and funding challenges facing the Executive, continue to be represented directly," she added.
The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it was "deeply frustrating" that the Northern Ireland executive would not be represented at the National Economic Council.
"I understand feelings are running high but it must be in the interests of the people of Northern Ireland that everyone gets round the table."
O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating last month's unnotified demonstrations in Portadown, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.
The Sinn Féin deputy leader has defended her involvement, saying it was the "right thing to do".
The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) leader Jim Allister said "the DUP's sham response today was beyond pathetic" adding "the DUP is interested only in clinging to office, not principle".
Alliance leader Naomi Long said refusing to attend or preventing others from attending the meeting with the prime minister was reckless and put party interests ahead of Northern Ireland's economic future and the needs of the public.
The Ulster Unionist Party leader Jon Burrows told BBC's Evening Extra programme the situation was a "political fudge" that was "all choreography and no consequences," adding that the move would "probably galvanise Sinn Féin further at the ballot box."
The Social Democratic and Labour Party's (SDLP) Matthew O'Toole said "plunging this place into more political chaos is not a sensible strategic move for unionism".
"Ultimately it's only going to make reasonable people here conclude that the largest unionist party simply doesn't want to make the status quo work," he added.
The DUP has been under pressure from unionist rivals and some within its own ranks over how to respond to the row over Drumcree.
Last week, DUP MP Carla Lockhart stepped down from the party's officer board over their leader Gavin Robinson not withdrawing Little-Pengelly to force O'Neill from their joint Stormont office.
On Thursday Lockhart said she will follow her "own course" if the party does not seek to remove Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill as Stormont's first minister.
Robinson said that while O'Neill and her party colleagues "should be punished, that does not include punishing the rest of Northern Ireland".
The Upper Bann MP, who last week quit the DUP's ruling officer board in opposition to party leader Gavin Robinson's approach, outlined her position in a letter to colleagues which she later posted on Facebook.
Other DUP representatives including assembly member Diane Forsythe have since backed Lockhart's calls for O'Neill to be "removed from office".
On Tuesday, Forsythe said that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".
On Wednesday, a second DUP assembly member called for O'Neill to go.
Maurice Bradley said removing O'Neill "would not, in itself, require the Assembly to collapse".
Bradley added that the party "must stand together" and "support Carla Lockhart".
Other party members including former MP Lord McCrea and Mid Ulster councillor Clement Cuthbertson have also backed Lockhart.
Party leader Robinson said last week that he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".
Speaking on the BBC's The View programme, Robinson said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.
He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".
"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.
Last week, a court heard Police Service of Northern Ireland intelligence information that dissidents may have mounted gun attacks on police had officers cleared a path for the parade.

title: US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you
content_c:
US interest rates held steady and economy grows - what it means for you
- Published
The US Federal Reserve has held interest rates steady at 3.75% - 4%.
The decision comes within a week of the midterm elections and after the central bank raised interest rates for the first time in three years at its September meeting.
"The overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgement, is that what we've done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said, referring to September's interest rate rise.
Figures published after the Fed's announcement showed the US economy growing at a stronger pace than expected, with inflation running above the Fed's target.
What is the Federal Reserve rate?
An interest rate tells people and businesses how much it costs to borrow money – such as with credit cards, mortgages, or business loans – but also what return they get for saving cash.
The Fed influences interest rates in the US through its target range for the federal funds rate, which is the interest rate used by commercial banks for overnight borrowing.
What's happening with US interest rates?
In its decision to hold rates steady this month, the Fed said that while inflation remains high, it wanted to gather more information before making another decision to change rates.
The Fed also noted that while there was uncertainty, the US economy remained resilient.
Warsh acknowledged that inflation remained too high, but noted that there were other signs - such as tightening credit conditions - that the economy was moving in the right direction.
There is plenty more economic data to come between now and the committee's next meeting, the Fed chair added, which should paint a more detailed picture of the state of the economy.
At that point, Warsh said, "we'll be, I think, better positioned to determine the right policy decision and the stance of policy."
While last month the committee signalled there could be one more rate rise this year, Warsh would not be drawn out on where he thinks they will go in six weeks' time.
"A lot of things can happen, so I'm not going to be able to share with you my musings."
The decision to hold rates steady was not unanimous.
While 10 of the 12 committee members voted to keep rates unchanged, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack voted to increase rates to 4%-4.25%, from its current 3.75%-4%.
The bank's next meeting will be held over 8-9 December.
What is happening in the US economy?
Warsh said things are moving in the right direction, while the US economy is performing very strongly.
The US economy grew by 3.4% on an annualised basis in the three months to September, stronger than analysts had expected.
That strong growth was driven by an acceleration in investment, and strong consumer spending.
While there was an annualised increase in personal spending of 3.8%, the annualised increase in private investment was a huge 19.4% which analysts say was largely due to investment in artificial intelligence.
Inflation is also above the Fed's target range.
Prices increased by 3.7% in the year to September, driven higher by fuel and energy prices which have surged off the back of the war in Iran.
How does the Fed rate affect mortgages, credit cards, and savings?
The Fed uses interest rate changes to try to keep inflation – the rate at which prices change – at 2% a year and keep the job market stable.
When inflation is too high, the Fed tends to raise interest rates.
This tends to mean higher rates from banks and other lenders, which in turn affects spending and saving decisions.
For example, someone refinancing their mortgage or buying a property for the first time could face higher mortgage rates. It could also mean higher interest rates on credit cards or car loans. However, it means higher interest rates on savings as well.
This encourages people and businesses to save more, spend less money, and make less investments. It also encourages companies to hire less people or slow the pace of pay rises.
All of this tends to reduce demand and slow inflation.
When inflation is low or if the Fed believes the economy needs a boost, it cut rates.
The idea is that this will have the opposite affect, with banks dropping rates leading to more spending and less saving from people and businesses.
Leaving the rates unchanged means rates on things like new mortgages or business loans are also less likely to change. It also means interest rates on cash savings are unlikely to rise.
How much have US interest rates changed?
US interest rates have historically moved around quite a bit.
The last time Fed rates were as high as they have been recently was in the lead up to and during the start of the 2008 global financial crisis.
The Fed then dropped rates to historic lows to encourage spending and job creation during the economic slump and kept them at those lows for several years.
They picked up again ahead of the pandemic before dropping to as low as 0%-0.25% during the pandemic. They then rose to highs of 5.25%-5% from the middle of 2023 to August 2024 as inflation jumped.
They had been falling steadily since then, until rates were raised last month.

title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
content_c:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

title: Female Lib Dem MP accuses Nigel Farage of shoving her in parliament
content_c:
A female Liberal Democrat MP has accused Nigel Farage of shoving her aside at the state opening of parliament after which one of her male colleagues intervened.
Caroline Voaden gave her account of the incident in May this year after Farage revealed on Wednesday that there had been a “physical altercation” in parliament which meant he had decided to avoid the budget.
Voaden told the Guardian: “He was trying to get out of the chamber and instead of just asking if he could go past, he said: ‘Let me past’. I turned round and said: ‘No, you can wait your turn like everyone else’. He grabbed me by the arm or the shoulder, pushed me to one side and tried to push past me. One of my colleagues tried to stop him because he thought I was going to fall down the stairs. And then we all shuffled down.
“Quite deliberately, he grabbed me by the arm from behind and pushed me to one side so that I fell into a colleague or the wall on the other side. I was really taken aback and really angry because I think you just don’t behave like that in any workplace, let alone the chamber of the House of Commons. It was rude. It was nasty.”
Voaden said she had complained to the serjeant at arms who she believed had written to Farage asking him to apologise. She also raised it with the speaker. “Nothing ever came of it,” she said.
A Reform UK source said it was “not true at all, it was the Lib Dem MPs being aggressive towards Nigel. This is typical Lib Dem dishonesty in an attempt to stay relevant.”
The male Lib Dem MP who intervened is understood to be Max Wilkinson, with sources saying he put a hand on Farage’s shoulder, “fairly gently” grabbed him and said he could not do that to another MP.
Reform sources also suggested a video from the Commons showed her account was wrong, but the Lib Dems said the incident took place before the footage started.
The row erupted after the Reform leader said he had skipped John Healey’s budget speech in the Commons on Wednesday because his seat reservation had been moved and he decided to give it a “wide berth” in order to “avoid conflict” in the chamber.
He claimed he had been involved in a “physical altercation” with another MP on the day of the state opening of parliament in May.
It later emerged his reservation had been removed by Commons staff as it did not have the proper date stamp.
Daisy Cooper, the Lib Dem deputy leader, told Sky News on Thursday morning that her party’s MPs were involved in the May incident mentioned by Farage.
She said: “My understanding – I didn’t see it, I wasn’t there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that.
“I didn’t see it, I didn’t witness what happened, but that was several months ago.
“And let’s be really clear: it’s Reform UK that had a problem at their conference with bundling female journalists and members out of their hall. So, we’ll take no lessons from them on this.”
Afterwards, Voaden posted on social media in response to Farage’s claim that he was at risk of “another physical altercation”: “We both know that’s not true Nigel don’t we?
“I’m still waiting for the apology you were required to write to me … Though I won’t hold my breath.”
When asked for a response to the accusations, Robert Jenrick, Reform’s shadow chancellor, said: “You know what? I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates.
“The thing about Reform politicians is, yeah, we love parliament, the institution of parliament. I go there every day. I speak in parliament. I represent my constituents.
“But I’m much more interested about, actually, the issues, trying to change this country, getting out and about outside of the bubble. And I’m not interested in even responding, dignifying the nonsense that Daisy Cooper is talking about there.”

title: Venezuela: Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado says US backs 2027 election
content_c:
Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado says US backs 2027 election
October 30, 2026
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday that the country was moving towards a US-prescribed presidential election in 2027, in her first public remarks since returning from 10 months in exile.
Calling the transition to democracy "irreversible," Machado said, "US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that includes presidential elections in 2027."
"The date of the election is the date of liberation," Machado said in Caracas after returning home following 10 months in exile.
Machado also reiterated that her priorities included dismantling the country's repressive system and securing the release of the thousands of political prisoners. She denied having had any contact with interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
Shortly before Machado's public statements, Rodriguez announced that there "will be elections" in Venezuela, without specifying a date.
Machado says Trump helped open 'floodgate to freedom'
Machado, who famously "presented" US President Donald Trump with her Nobel Peace Prize, thanked Trump for his actions on January 3, leading to "the floodgate to freedom" being opened in Venezuela.
The opposition leader was referring to the US capture of former President Nicolas Maduro, currently facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.
Machado, however, criticized a major oil deal Washington and Caracas agreed to earlier this year, under which Venezuela is expected to supply 20% of its oil reserves to the United States.
"This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants," she said.
At the same time, she skirted questions that highlighted Trump's comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, as well as his suggestion this week that the country could become the 51st US state.
US caught in a bind
Machado, who was barred from contesting the 2024 presidential election, backed opposition candidate Edmundo Gonzalez. His supporters said he had won by a wide margin, even though electoral authorities declared Maduro the winner.
Machado's recent return after nearly a year in exile complicates things for Washington which has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but also praised acting President Rodriguez.

title: Oppositionspolitikerin Machado: Was bedeutet ihre Rückkehr für Venezuela?
content_c:
Oppositionspolitikerin Was bedeutet die Rückkehr von Machado für Venezuela?
Die venezolanische Oppositionspolitikerin María Corina Machado ist aus dem Exil zurückgekehrt. Dort ermittelt die Justiz gegen sie wegen Vaterlandverrats - doch sie versteckt sich nicht mehr.
Als María Corina Machado am Sonntagabend in einem Auto stehend durch Caracas fährt, wird sie vom Jubel ihrer Anhänger begleitet. Sie winkt ihren Unterstützern zu, die zu Tausenden an den Straßen stehen.
Machado genießt in Umfragen noch immer die meisten Zustimmungswerte. Diese Popularität will sie nutzen, wie sie bei einer Pressekonferenz am Donnerstag in Caracas sagt.
"Das Regime kennt mich, sie wissen, dass ich mein Wort halte. Und ein in einem Verhandlungsprozess gegebenes Wort wird eingehalten und darauf setzt das Land und darauf hofft die Mehrheit."
Vielzahl an Ermittlungen gegen Machado
Eigentlich drohte der Oppositionspolitikerin bei einer Einreise die Festnahme. Eine Reihe von Ermittlungen - wegen Terrorismus, Verschwörung, Anstiftung zu Gewalt und Aufruhr, Beteiligung an Attentatsplänen und Vaterlandsverrat. Das zumindest wurde ihr von Venezuelas regimetreuer Justiz vorgeworfen. Aufgehoben wurden sie bislang nicht.
"Ich habe keinen Freipass, keine Garantie, keine Botschaft und kein Signal erhalten. Die Aufhebung des Simón-Bolívar-Gesetzes, des Hass- und Terrorismusgesetzes sind eine absolute Priorität. Sie werden weiterhin als Drohung eingesetzt, nicht gegen mich, denn es geht hier nicht um mich, sondern um Millionen von Venezolanern."
Doch auch wenn Übergangspräsidentin Delcy Rodríguez abfällig auf Machados Rückkehr reagierte, ihren Auftritt als "Show" bezeichnete - ansonsten hält sie sich zurück, Drohungen bleiben aus. Kurz vor Machados Pressekonferenz hält Delcy - wie sie in Venezuela nur genannt wird - eine Botschaft an die Nation. Und präsentiert sich darin als Garantin für die Demokratie.
"Wir müssen einen Rahmen finden für Frieden und echtes demokratisches Zusammenleben, eine geordnete Rechtsreform und faire Teilhabe aller politischen Kräfte des Landes. Und für Wahlen, die eine Lösung darstellen und nicht zu unüberbrückbaren Konflikten führen."
Spiel auf Zeit - USA als Faktor?
Ein Datum für Wahlen nennt sie dabei nicht. Für Jesus Renzullo, Venezolaner und Politikwissenschaftler am GIGA-Institut in Berlin, reines Kalkül. "Caracas zieht es vor, seine Feinde und politischen Rivalen nicht auszuschalten, sondern sie zu schwächen, indem es ihren Handlungsspielraum einschränkt, bis die Proteste und Versprechen eines Wandels unter ihrem eigenen Gewicht zusammenbrechen." Ein Spiel auf Zeit - das auch die USA mitspielen.
"Washington profitiert von der Regierung unter Delcy Rodríguez, möchte aber gleichzeitig den Eindruck aufrechterhalten, dass die Vereinigten Staaten sich für einen Machtwechsel einsetzen", sagt Renzullo.
Verzögerung aus Eigeninteresse
"Washington will Rodríguez’ Amtszeit so lange wie möglich verlängern, um von den Vorzugsbedingungen zu profitieren, die die Regierung Rodríguez amerikanischen Unternehmen in allen Wirtschaftsbereichen des Landes gewährt."
Neben Interesse am Öl wird das auch in anderen Sektoren deutlich, so Renzullo: Medikamenten, Bergbauprojekten, öffentlichen Ausschreibungen, bei denen die USA den Zuschlag bekommen sollen.
Beide Seiten, USA wie Übergangsregierung in Venezuela, verzögern den Prozess eines stabilen Übergangs aus Eigeninteressen. So bleibt Machado die populärste Stimme der venezolanischen Opposition, doch vorerst nur mit einem Pfund in der Hand: dem Druck der Straße, solange er hält.

title: 65 Jahre deutsch-türkisches Anwerbeabkommen – die Altersarmut der Gastarbeiter
content_c:
65 Jahre später sind viele Gastarbeiter von damals arm
29. Oktober 2026
Der Ort war bewusst gewählt: Am Düsseldorfer Flughafen dankte der nordrhein-westfälische Ministerpräsident Henrik Wüst Mitte September mit einem Festakt den Menschen, die dort 65 Jahre zuvor aus dem Flieger gestiegen waren. Den Gastarbeiterinnen und Gastarbeitern der ersten Generation, die das Abenteuer gewagt, ihre Heimat zurückgelassen und am Ende ihren Teil zum Wohlstand der Bundesrepublik beigetragen hatten.
Allein 870.000 Türkinnen und Türken waren es bis zum Anwerbestopp 1973 – sie schufteten in den Bergbauzechen, leisteten Akkordarbeit an den Fließbändern oder putzten die Fabrikhallen. Die meisten von ihnen blieben und fanden in Düsseldorf, Köln oder Duisburg ihr neues Zuhause. "Sie haben unser Land vielfältiger, offener und stärker gemacht", lobte Wüst, stellte aber auch klar: "Erst wenn Name, Hautfarbe und Religion keine Rolle mehr spielen, sind wir am Ziel."
Doch davon sei Deutschland immer noch ein Stück weit entfernt, sagt Haci-Halil Uslucan der DW, weil es auch 65 Jahre später noch sehr viel Diskriminierung gegenüber Türkeistämmigen gebe. Dabei sei das Abkommen eigentlich eine Erfolgsgeschichte: "Wir haben in vielen Bereichen Erfolge, also Bildungsaufstiege. Wir haben heute eine Vielzahl von Universitätsabsolventen, wir haben berufliche Aufstiege. Wir haben auch politische Aufstiege, den baden-württembergischen Ministerpräsidenten Cem Özdemir beispielsweise."
Altersarmut bei Migranten deutlich höher
Uslucan selbst ist das perfekte Beispiel: Sein Vater kam nach 1971 nach Berlin und arbeitete in der Textilbranche, zwei Jahre später holte er seine Frau und seine beiden Söhne nach. Haci-Halil Uslucan promovierte im Fach Psychologie und ist heute Professor für Moderne Türkeistudien an der Universität Duisburg Essen. Eines seiner jüngsten Forschungsthemen handelt von den Schattenseiten des Anwerbeabkommens, dass viele der damaligen Gastarbeiter betrifft und umtreibt: die Einsamkeit älterer Zuwanderer. Doch nicht nur das Alleinsein macht einigen Türkeistämmigen im Rentenalter zunehmend zu schaffen.
"Altersarmut ist, das zeigen die Studien, bei Migranten doppelt so hoch, zwischen 25 und 30 Prozent gegenüber 12 bis 14 Prozent bei den Deutschen. Die Invaliditätsrate und die Frühverrentung ist bei Migranten deutlich höher, weil die erste Generation sehr stark körperlich gearbeitet hatte." Auch die Wahrscheinlichkeit, zehn Jahre vor dem Rentenalter arbeitslos zu werden, sei doppelt so hoch, so Uslucan. "Zudem haben sie ein niedrigeres Monatseinkommen, häufig unterbrochene Lebensläufe und im Niedriglohnsektor gearbeitet. Folglich ist auch ihre Rente gering."
Rente fällt um 360 Euro niedriger aus
Eine Sonderauswertung der Deutschen Rentenversicherung für den Mediendienst Integration kommt zu alarmierenden Zahlen: Rentenempfänger mit türkischer Staatsangehörigkeit erhalten in Deutschland im Schnitt etwa 360 Euro weniger Rente als deutsche Rentenempfänger: Ende 2025 waren es 890 Euro im Vergleich zu 1.250 Euro pro Monat. Noch beunruhigender: Der Anteil von Personen mit türkischer Staatsangehörigkeit, die hier Grundsicherung im Alter erhalten, war im Juni 2026 mehr als dreimal so hoch wie bei Deutschen (9,3 zu 2,7 Prozent).
Sozialwissenschaftler Eric Seils von der Hans-Böckler-Stiftung in Düsseldorf sagt der DW, viele der Gastarbeiter wären schon älter nach Deutschland gekommen und hätten so weniger in die Rentenkasse einzahlen können: "Der wichtigste Grund sind natürlich die früheren Löhne, die frühere Arbeitsgeschichte. Die Gastarbeiter, die nach Deutschland gekommen sind, sind oft direkt in die Fabrik, in den Bergbau oder auf den Bau gegangen. Dort haben sie keine hohen Stundenlöhne bekommen, weil sie häufig schlechter gebildet waren als die Deutschen."
Mit der Deindustrialisierung Anfang der 70er Jahre und der Ölkrise hätten zudem viele Gastarbeiter ihren Job verloren. "Damit waren nicht mehr so gute Jobs bei den klassischen Industriebetrieben vorhanden. Wer nicht so gut gebildet war, wurde dann eher arbeitslos als Menschen mit Bildung, bei den Deutschen war es genauso. Und wenn Erwerbskarrieren unterbrochen werden, schlägt sich das natürlich irgendwann in der Rente nieder."
Gastarbeiter konnten sich kaum weiterqualifizieren
Auch Janina Söhn vom Soziologischen Forschungsinstitut Göttingen (SOFI) an der Georg-August-Universität hat sich mit dem Thema Altersarmut von Zugewanderten beschäftigt. Ihr Fazit: Dass fast ein Drittel der Menschen, die zugewandert sind, armutsgefährdet seien, sei ein großes Problem in Deutschland. "Diese Gruppe trifft es noch härter als zum Beispiel Frauen im Allgemeinen, die auch schon ein erhöhtes Armutsrisiko haben. Wenn man dann auf alleinlebende Migrantinnen schaut, sind das ganz schlimme, alarmierende Zahlen. Wenn es da keine familiäre Unterstützung gäbe, wäre das alles noch viel trauriger."
Auch die Möglichkeit, im Rentenalter selbst noch ein paar Euro dazuzuverdienen, ist vielen Menschen mit türkischer Staatsangehörigkeit häufig versperrt. Sei es, weil ihre oftmals geringe Qualifikation nicht ausreicht, oder aber weil sie durch ihre harte körperliche Arbeit in jungen Jahren nicht mehr dazu in der Lage sind. Laut Zahlen der Bundesagentur für Arbeit ist ihre Beschäftigungsquote nur halb so hoch wie bei den Deutschen (5,2 zu 10,8 Prozent). Söhn sagt:
"Im Grunde ist das eine ganze Summe von Benachteiligungen oder von Härten im Leben. Die Generation der Gastarbeiter wurde ja von Deutschland geholt, hat dann hier die schlimmsten Jobs gemacht, während sich die Einheimischen zum Teil herausqualifizieren konnten." Für die Gastarbeiter dagegen habe es keine Weiterbildungsinitiativen gegeben. "Die Menschen, die diese harten Jobs gemacht haben, die auch immer für jede Wirtschaft notwendig sind, haben es mit ihrer Gesundheit bezahlt."

title: Чи приїде тепер таксі Києва на дешеві замовлення: що змінилося
content_c:
Чи приїде тепер таксі Києва на дешеві замовлення: що змінилося
Як працюватиме таксі Києва під час обмеження цін на поїздки у тривоги — експерт, водій та постійні пасажири зробили прогноз.
Після того, як уряд зробив намагання обмежити ціни на поїздки в таксі Києва під час тривог і транспортних форс-мажорів, експерти, безпосередньо самі таксисти та постійні пасажири висловили свої думки про можливі плюси та ризики такого нововведення.
Нагадаємо, як відомо, прем’єр-міністр України Сергій Корецький повідомив, що урядовий меморандум з операторами служб таксі передбачає встановлення стелі, до якої може піднятися ціна за таких умов. Це максимум 75% до базового тарифу.
«Тобто якщо базовий тариф за звичних умов — без тривог, заторів тощо — з точки А в точку Б становить умовно 200 грн, то максимальна плата буде 350 грн. Якщо 300 грн — то максимум 525 грн. Пасажири зберігають можливість самим регулювати ціну, але будуть також встановлені граничні межі», — повідомив Корецький.
Своєю чергою, експерт з питань роботи столичного транспорту Олександр Гречко в коментарі для ТСН.ua висловив думку про те, що з однією сторони позитивна новина про обмеження цін на поїздки в таксі може мати і абсолютно зворотній бік.
«Уряд домовився з компаніями, щоб вони нібито не підвищували ціни. Начебто добра справа. По-перше: це стосується дуже незначного періоду, періоду повітряних тривог червоного рівня. Плюс 2 години після закінчення тривоги. В цей час кількість таксистів не збільшується, але у людей з’являється більше потреб кудись доїхати. Особливо вранці або ввечері або якщо погана погода, коли попит збільшується в рази, а пропозицій більше не стає. Відповідно, за цих умов людина, яка може дозволити заплатити більше за таксі, ставить більшу вартість, на цю ціну водій погоджується. Я підписався на чат таксистів, вони глибоко незадоволені нововведенням. З урахуванням того, що місто часто стоїть у заторах і якщо обмежують дохід від поїздки, їм подекуди вигідніше або дочекатись того часу, коли обмежень не буде, або брати замовлення не на інший берег столиці, а по району. Або когось „підхопити“ без замовлення, наприклад, біля станції метро. Виходить так, що пасажир може довго шукати того, хто погодиться або махати рукою, зупиняючи автівки. Водії таксі не захочуть стояти у заторах, витрачати бензин заради того, щоб заробити умовно кажучи 200 гривень», — каже Олександр Гречко.
На його думку, ситуацію міг би частково вирішити громадський транспорт, якщо б він не був змушений стояти у заторах.
«Щоб громадський транспорт не стояв у заторах, треба залучати патрулі поліції, аби вони контролювали смуги для цього транспорту», — припускає він.
На цю тему Олександр Гречко написав відповідний допис у соцмережі. Одним з перших месенджів він зазначив наступне: «Драйвери/водії будуть брати менше замовлень в додатках, якщо там цінова стеля буде 500 грн за якусь поїздку, а людина на вулиці махне рукою і запропонує 800-1000 готівки чи на картку».
Один з тих, хто прокоментував цей пост, відрекомендувався таксистом, який працює з 1999 року.
«Бізнес підписав, от нехай бізнес і возить. А водії — це не бізнес, це окремі суб’єкти, які не будуть грати в ігри, там де їм не цікаво. Я в таксі з 1999 року», — написав користувач Ігор.
Олександр Гречко каже, що навіть у такій ситуації є часткова альтернатива.
«Вранці 29 жовтня я їздив до Південного мосту подивитись на ситуацію. Люди дуже активно користуються прокатом електросамокатів — за 70 гривень можна за 10 хвилин подолати міст і не платити в декілька разів більше. І ще за декілька хвилин доїхати на метро до центру міста. Тобто є така альтернатива. У середньому заряду самоката може вистачити на 15-20 кілометрів поїздки», — каже він.
Таксі Києва: що кажуть постійні пасажири
ТСН.ua поспілкувався з декількома киянами, які частіше середнього користуються послугами таксі.
«У мене бувають такі ситуації, це коли заздалегідь є попередження з багатьох джерел про ракетну атаку, то я на таксі можу поїхати до гарного укриття. Якщо ніхто не погоджується на додаткові 100 гривень, я додаю 250 гривень до базової вартості поїздки. Звісно, що таке відбувається не часто, а коли є попередження від американської розвідки про масовану атаку. Я взяла за правило прямувати до укриття», — розповіла нам киянка Христина Бєлова.
До цього вона додає: «Крім того, у мене нещодавно була ситуація, коли за поїздку від станції метро «Арсенальна» до станції метро «Іподром» пізно ввечері я заплатила 1 тисячу гривень, хоча базова ціна була значно меншою. Але за меншу ціну ніхто не хотів їхати. Я ніколи не користуюсь послугами випадкових автівок, завжди замовляю у додатку».
Ще один з киян, який часто користується послугами таксі, нам в коментарі розповів, що протягом останнього часу, коли повітряні тривоги значно почастішали, доводиться підвищувати ціну.
«Вимушеною буденністю стало те, що у часи пік додаю до вартості поїздки 200-250 гривень, щоб доїхати з центра міста до Софіївської Борщагівки. Тобто на звичайну базову ціну, хоч вона і чимала, мало хто погоджується, а їхати треба», — розповів нам цей чоловік.
Нагадаємо, раніше повідомлялось про те, що понтони через Дніпро не врятують Київ від транспортного колапсу. Після пошкодження Південного мосту в Києві влада готує альтернативні переправи через Дніпро, проте понтони, насипні дамби та плавучі платформи мають технічні обмеження.

Особливо вранці або ввечері або якщо погана погода, коли попит збільшується в рази, а пропозицій більше не стає. Відповідно, за цих умов людина, яка може дозволити заплатити більше за таксі, ставить більшу вартість, на цю ціну водій погоджується. Я підписався на чат таксистів, вони глибоко незадоволені нововведенням. З урахуванням того, що місто часто стоїть у заторах і якщо обмежують дохід від поїздки, їм подекуди вигідніше або дочекатись того часу, коли обмежень не буде, або брати замовлення не на інший берег столиці, а по району. Або когось „підхопити“ без замовлення, наприклад, біля станції метро. Виходить так, що пасажир може довго шукати того, хто погодиться або махати рукою, зупиняючи автівки. Водії таксі не захочуть стояти у заторах, витрачати бензин заради того, щоб заробити умовно кажучи 200 гривень», — каже Олександр Гречко.
На його думку, ситуацію міг би частково вирішити громадський транспорт, якщо б він не був змушений стояти у заторах.
«Щоб громадський транспорт не стояв у заторах, треба залучати патрулі поліції, аби вони контролювали смуги для цього транспорту», — припускає він.
На цю тему Олександр Гречко написав відповідний допис у соцмережі. Одним з перших месенджів він зазначив наступне: «Драйвери/водії будуть брати менше замовлень в додатках, якщо там цінова стеля буде 500 грн за якусь поїздку, а людина на вулиці махне рукою і запропонує 800-1000 готівки чи на картку».
Один з тих, хто прокоментував цей пост, відрекомендувався таксистом, який працює з 1999 року.
«Бізнес підписав, от нехай бізнес і возить. А водії — це не бізнес, це окремі суб’єкти, які не будуть грати в ігри, там де їм не цікаво. Я в таксі з 1999 року», — написав користувач Ігор.
Олександр Гречко каже, що навіть у такій ситуації є часткова альтернатива.
«Вранці 29 жовтня я їздив до Південного мосту подивитись на ситуацію. Люди дуже активно користуються прокатом електросамокатів — за 70 гривень можна за 10 хвилин подолати міст і не платити в декілька разів більше. І ще за декілька хвилин доїхати на метро до центру міста. Тобто є така альтернатива. У середньому заряду самоката може вистачити на 15-20 кілометрів поїздки», — каже він.
Таксі Києва: що кажуть постійні пасажири
ТСН.ua поспілкувався з декількома киянами, які частіше середнього користуються послугами таксі.
«У мене бувають такі ситуації, це коли заздалегідь є попередження з багатьох джерел про ракетну атаку, то я на таксі можу поїхати до гарного укриття. Якщо ніхто не погоджується на додаткові 100 гривень, я додаю 250 гривень до базової вартості поїздки. Звісно, що таке відбувається не часто, а коли є попередження від американської розвідки про масовану атаку. Я взяла за правило прямувати до укриття», — розповіла нам киянка Христина Бєлова.
До цього вона додає: «Крім того, у мене нещодавно була ситуація, коли за поїздку від станції метро «Арсенальна» до станції метро «Іподром» пізно ввечері я заплатила 1 тисячу гривень, хоча базова ціна була значно меншою. Але за меншу ціну ніхто не хотів їхати. Я ніколи не користуюсь послугами випадкових автівок, завжди замовляю у додатку».
Ще один з киян, який часто користується послугами таксі, нам в коментарі розповів, що протягом останнього часу, коли повітряні тривоги значно почастішали, доводиться підвищувати ціну.
«Вимушеною буденністю стало те, що у часи пік додаю до вартості поїздки 200-250 гривень, щоб доїхати з центра міста до Софіївської Борщагівки. Тобто на звичайну базову ціну, хоч вона і чимала, мало хто погоджується, а їхати треба», — розповів нам цей чоловік.
Нагадаємо, раніше повідомлялось про те, що понтони через Дніпро не врятують Київ від транспортного колапсу. Після пошкодження Південного мосту в Києві влада готує альтернативні переправи через Дніпро, проте понтони, насипні дамби та плавучі платформи мають технічні обмеження.

title: Все еще острый: в итальянском озере нашли меч возрастом 3300 лет
content_c:
Археологи обнаружили в вулканическом озере в Италии хорошо сохранившийся бронзовый меч. Исследователи оценили его возраст в 3300 лет, вероятно, оружие было подношением божеству или принадлежало высокопоставленному воину, жившему задолго до появления этрусков или римлян, сообщает Live Science.
Меч нашли в озере Меццано. Оружие относится к позднему бронзовому веку (XIV–XIII века до н. э.) и до сих пор остается острым. Это уже третий подобный меч, найденный в озере Меццано за последние 50 лет.
В эпоху бронзы на месте нынешнего озера Меццано люди строили жилища на сваях; в ходе недавних исследований археологи обнаружили остатки этого затонувшего поселения. Исследователи также обнаружили множество целых сосудов, топоры, наконечники стрел, кинжалы, наконечники копий, булавки и бронзовую бритву.
Меч и бритва были найдены рядом друг с другом. Ученые считают, что оба объекта принадлежали человеку высокого социального статуса — например, элитному воину. Исследователи отмечают, что присутствие металлического оружия в озере может быть связано и с более широкой ритуальной практикой эпохи бронзы, в рамках которой в водоемы бросали целые клады: украшения, а также намеренно согнутые или «убитые» (ритуально выведенные из строя) предметы. Эта традиция сохранялась на протяжении столетий вплоть до эпохи этрусков, когда колодцы ритуально «закрывали», помещая в них различные артефакты, а иногда и принося человеческие жертвы.
В XIII веке до н. э. жители Центральной Италии были включены в торговые сети, охватывавшие все Средиземноморье. Бронзовое оружие в те времена было не только средством ведения боя, но и символом престижа, принадлежности к определенной группе и власти.
Недавно археологи из Европейского института подводной археологии и Министерства туризма и древностей Египта обнаружили кольцо, на котором был выгравирован Александрийский маяк – одно из семи чудес древнего мира.

title: У турецькій Каппадокії обвалилися скелі, загинули люди. Цей регіон приваблює туристів з усього світу
content_c:
У турецькій Каппадокії обвалилися скелі, загинули люди. Цей регіон приваблює туристів з усього світу
  - Author, Ярослав Луків
  - Role, ВВС
- Published
- Час прочитання: 2 хв
Щонайменше троє людей загинули, ще п'ятеро поранені після обвалу скель на популярному туристичному об'єкті в Каппадокії в Туреччині.
Про це повідомив губернатор провінції Невшехір Хюсейн Кьок. Тіло третьої жертви витягли з-під каміння нещодавно.
За повідомленнями, зруйнувався один зі шпилів скель, відомих як "казкові димарі".
Міністр юстиції попередив, що під уламками можуть бути ще люди.
Причина інциденту наразі невідома, однак місцеві ЗМІ повідомили, що обвал могли спричинити сильні дощі, які нещодавно випали у регіоні.
На відеозаписі інциденту видно, що біля парковки велика територія, вкрита пилом.
Триває пошуково-рятувальна операція.
Регіон Каппадокія приваблює туристів з усього світу, які хочуть побачити стародавні "казкові димарі" або "димарі фей" — високі конусоподібні скельні утворення, що виникли внаслідок вулканічної діяльності.
Скелі незвичної форми у Каппадокії утворилися мільйони років тому, коли відкладення попелу з діючих вулканів були розмиті дощем і вітром.

title: Російська атака реактивним безпілотником спричинила пожежу в Основ'янському районі Харкова – Терехов
content_c:
Війська РФ у п'ятницю завдали удару реактивним безпілотником по Основ'янському району Харкова, внаслідок чого на місці влучання спалахнула пожежа, повідомив міський голова Харкова Ігор Терехов у п'ятницю.
"Ворог атакував реактивним БПЛА Основ'янський район. На місці влучання – пожежа. Інформація про постраждалих наразі не надходила. Наслідки з'ясовуємо", – написав мер у своєму телеграм-каналі.
За словами Терехова, звернення щодо потерпілих унаслідок ворожого удару на цей час відсутні, профільні служби встановлюють масштаби пошкоджень.

title: Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
content_c:
Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
- Published
The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

title: Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
content_c:
Lib Dems and Reform UK in war of words over alleged shove
- Published
A war of words has broken out between Lib Dem MP Caroline Voaden and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage over an alleged physical altercation in the House of Commons.
The row was triggered when Farage, explaining why he had not attended Wednesday's Budget, said he had been involved in a "physical altercation" with another MP at the State Opening of Parliament in May and had wanted to avoid a similar incident.
Voaden revealed herself to be the MP Farage had been referring to, writing on social media that she had been left "shocked and bloody angry" by the confrontation.
The Lib Dems have claimed that Farage "attempted to shove" their South Devon MP but a Reform source accused the party of "lying".
The Reform insider added: "The Lib Dems were claiming Nigel shoved her and that she was shaken, the video disproves that clearly."
Footage, first unearthed by the Daily Telegraph, shows the pair leaving the chamber together at the state opening of Parliament but there is no visible evidence of a major altercation.
However, Voaden has said the incident between herself and Farage was not shown in the clip originally posted by the Telegraph, external.
The incident does not appear to have been captured on the official feed of the state opening provided by Parliament.
Voaden said Farage had been ordered to apologise to her after she complained to Commons authorities. The House of Commons would not comment on this.
In a statement, Voaden said: "The truth is that on the day of the King's Speech, Farage missed his chance to process with the other party leaders to the Lords, and rather than queue with the rest of us, he shoved me out of the way to barge past.
"Such behaviour is unacceptable in any workplace, and it has no place in the House of Commons.
"Shoving a colleague out of the way on a staircase just shows the complete disdain he has for Parliament and for other MPs."
Asked about the incident on Sky News, Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "My understanding - I didn't see it, I wasn't there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that."
Reform MP Robert Jenrick told Sky: "I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates."
The issue has only now emerged, nearly six months after the alleged incident, because Farage was pressed on why he had not been in the House of Commons chamber for the Budget on Wednesday.
In response he said: "At the State Opening of Parliament, I got involved… I didn't want to… but I got involved in a physical altercation with an MP in the chamber.
"I didn't make a fuss about it, I didn't complain, but I could see given that my prayer card had been removed, I was heading towards another physical altercation.
A spokesperson for the House of Commons said that a prayer card for Farage - the way in which MPs reserve seats in the Commons - did not "display a valid date stamp" and therefore "was removed in line with the usual Chamber protocol".

title: From workshops to the catwalk - why mended clothes are going mainstream
content_c:
From workshops to the catwalk - why mended clothes are going mainstream
- Published
If Alice Brown is browsing in second-hand shops and finds a jumper with a hole, that won't stop her buying it.
"I see it as challenge," says the 27-year-old forest ranger from Lincolnshire.
She is a champion of the growing fashion for eye-catching repairs.
Over the last year she has developed her own unique style, needle-felting cute animals and insects to cover moth holes, stains and other imperfections, winning her a huge following online.
"The natural place for decoration is in the centre at the front. If the hole is under the arm or on the shoulder, it forces you to think about the design," she says.
Often dubbed "visible mending" the trend is spreading from hobby crafters and community workshops, even drawing in fast-fashion brands and reaching the designer catwalks this year.
At one Saturday morning workshop in Brighton, Jayne Eagle shows her students how to attach a patch of fabric behind a tear so the cat-face design peeps through.
Then she instructs them in stitching techniques inspired by the traditional Japanese methods Boro and Sashiko. Instead of matching the thread colour to the garment, they make the mend highly decorative using geometric patterns in large white stitching.
She also offers classes in darning using contrasting vibrant colours that celebrate, rather than disguise, the repair.
One student, Nicola, has already used her newfound skills to stitch over sunscreen marks on a T-shirt "making a feature of it" and is now delighted that people "stop seeing the stains and just see the decoration".
Another student, Lisa, says her mother's generation would never have wanted the mends to show. "Now part of it is being proud of what you've done," she says.
Lisa bought a second-hand jacket online, but snipped the fabric with the scissors when she was opening the package. She managed to patch it in a way that "looks intentional".
"I was actually pointing it out to people," she laughs.
In the past mending was primarily about saving money, by wearing clothes for longer, rather than buying new. But visible mending is about celebrating that choice.
The trend took off about six years ago, Jayne says, and has boomed since.
An era of "throwaway" fast fashion from the 1980s onwards undermined the tradition of looking after and mending your clothes and people lost the skills, she says.
The revival of interest feels to her like a backlash against overproduction in the fashion industry and the damage it causes: the pollution, carbon emissions, water use, and poor labour conditions.
So perhaps it is surprising just how popular mended style is proving among retailers, with brands from Ralph Lauren to ultra-fast-fashion firm Shein currently selling stitched and patched garments, albeit in both of those cases brand new off the peg.
Other High Street chains are adopting a more authentic approach, offering in-house repairs and workshops.
"We want to give customers practical ways to extend the life of the clothes they already love, rather than simply replacing them," says Uniqlo's head of sustainability, Maria Ledous.
Primark, often seen as a fast-fashion retailer due to its lower prices, has also joined the trend.
"We don't think that affordability and durability should be opposites," says Vicki Swain, the brand's longevity lead.
Outdoor brand Finisterre says around a fifth of the mends it provides for customers are designed to be eye-catching, while premium artisan clothing store Toast says around a third of customers go for that option.
Part of the "magic" is that customers can bring in a garment and "choose what they'd like it to become next", says Toast chief executive Suzie de Rohan Willner.
Toast's repair services are free, but off-the-peg "renewed" pieces fetch higher prices than the originals to reflect their unique character.
Levi's, which boasts probably the longest tradition of being fixed up by its fans using anything from rhinestones to fringed cuffs, is rolling out a workshop programme this year.
The firm says its research shows younger customers in particular want to repair more but don't know how.
For now, Levi's' workshops focus on traditional mending skills, such as sewing on a button and hemming, rather than visible mends, and at a recent launch event in London, that seemed to be what its Gen Z participants were looking for.
"I'm from East London. If you have holes in your clothes people are like 'Ha ha! You're poor!'," says 16-year-old school student Bianca.
Theo, 19, says he'd rather learn how to mend without it showing.
"I would want [the jeans] to look how I originally bought them," he says.
He has a side hustle selling clothes at car boot sales and thinks traditional repair skills would make it more lucrative.
His friend Nicholas, also 19, says most people want to look "fresh".
"No-one wants to look like they came out of a dumpster," he says.
Still, Paul Dillinger, Levi's head of global design innovation, thinks more creative repairs will win them over as they pick up more skills.
"No-one has time for that perfect 'straight from the shop' thing. That's not cool.
"People crave agency," he says. "Mending is a demonstration of humanity: it's not a mustard stain, it's a memory of a great day in the ballpark."

title: Cuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new song
content_c:
Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says the Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America.
In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.
Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”.
The move further escalated a feud with Canada that has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around. Adams’s lyrics emphasise the roots of the name:
 The ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her
It’s a First Nations name – not an executive order.
Adams’s lyrics also suggest that Trump’s naming stunt was intended to deflect from the president’s other political problems, including the war in Iran and renewed scrutiny of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
 But things weren’t going his way in Iran
So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram
But it feels like another distraction
While the Epstein files were getting traction
The song is part of what Adams described in a recent interview as a broader “love letter” to Canada: a songwriting project that began with an invitation from a film company to write about the Maritimes provinces of Canada and has since morphed into the upcoming album How’s It Goin’.
“After finishing the first song, I moved on to that one, and then moved on to another one, and then started thinking maybe I should just carry on with my theme,” he said.
As well as homages to Canadian heroes, the album also includes 51st State, released on 1 July – Canada Day – as another repudiation of Trump, in this case his efforts to annex Canada.
 You can push us to the brink
But where the open road divides
You’ll find a wall of maple
With us on the other side.
The first time he played the song in public was in the US.
“We weren’t sure how people were going to respond to it,” he said. “But we got a standing ovation every night for it. It made me think: perhaps, finally, the tide’s turning.”
