title: UK politics: Burnham denies preventing ministers from speaking about plans for closer relationship with EU – as it happened
content_c:
Burnham insists letter telling ministers not to argue for specific UK-EU renegotiation outcomes doesn't mean they're gagged
Andy Burnham has rejected claims that he has stopped ministers speaking out about his plans for a closer relationship with Europe.
As mentioned earlier (see 12.14pm), Burnham wrote to ministers yesterday saying he does not want them to “advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process” as he opens a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU. At GB News, this has been written up under the headline: “Andy Burnham gags Cabinet on rejoin EU plot”.
Asked if he was preventing ministers from speaking out in his pooled interview with broadcasters today, Burnham replied:
Not in the slightest. I have been working with the cabinet on the approach that we’re taking to Europe, and we have a clear approach now as we go into the next UK-EU summit, which is three weeks away.
For the record, this is what Burnham said in the letter sent to cabinet ministers yesterday.
I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain. It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration.
It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.
Burnham said that at the UK-EU summit on 20 November he wanted to lock in deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. But he said he would also set out the next steps for considering the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU. He went on:
Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.
I am also clear that any fundamental change to the direction of the relationship would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament.
Burnham said there was an “agreed mandate” in government for the summit. He went on:
In the period beyond the summit, government policy will be to explore options for the long-term relationship with the EU for consideration in the next parliament.
At the end of this process, we will set out to the country the respective merits and drawbacks of the various options.
It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period.
It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.
Streeting says Labour committee chair's criticism of defence spending in budget 'completely unfounded'
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has criticised the senior Labour MP Tan Dhesi for saying the government is not raising military spending quickly enough.
Dhesi is chair of the Commons defence committee and yesterday, in his capacity as committee chair, he issued a statement about the budget saying:
The defence committee is pleased that the defence investment plan has been fully funded in the budget, but we had hoped to see the chancellor set out a precise pathway to spending 3% - and eventually 3.5% - of GDP on defence. Instead, some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year’s spending review.
There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation’s defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass. Our adversaries are not bound by fiscal years and spending cycles. We need to urgently rebuild our capabilities now, or we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict.
Speaking in the Commons during the budget, Streeting referred to this statement saying:
I think that is completely unfounded criticism … It would be fair criticism if this government had not already made decisions that is leading to the fastest increase in defence spending since the end of the Cold War. Not in future years, already, on the basis of our first two years.
But Streeting also insisted Dhesi was “a good friend”.
Healey (66) says he does not expect UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime
Last year Andy Burnham told a Guardian podcast that he hopes to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime. He is currently 56, and he has recently said that he stands by this comment – although he has also stressed that this does not necessarily mean that he expects his proposed debate on a closer relationship with the EU to result in a proposal to rejoin after the election.
In his interview on Channel 4 News, John Healey, the chancellor, was also asked if he wanted Britain to rejoin in his lifetime. He replied:
I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that …
I expect, and my job is to try and make the most of Britain’s position now.
Healey confirms government not committed to bring down welfare bill before next election
John Healey, the chancellor, has now personally clarified that the government is not committed to bringing down the welfare bill before the next election. He did so in an interview with Channel 4 News, revising a message he gave out with an ambiguous answer in an interview with the Today programme. (See 9.23am.)
Asked if he was committed to reducing the welfare bill this parliament, he replied:
We’re certainly committed to bringing the cost of the welfare bill down. I’ve said that, the prime minister’s said that. It is not correct to say that we set any schedule or time limit for that.
Asked if that meant it would not come down this parliament, he replied:
It’s not correct to say that we’re going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.
Channel 4 News sent out a press release with the transcript headlined: “John Healey tells Krishnan Guru-Murthy Labour will not bring welfare bill down in this Parliament”. Healey’s not having much luck with media today because this does not seem 100% accurate either. He is saying the government has not committed to bringing the welfare bill down this parliament. But that is not the same as saying the government has committed to not bringing it down. In practice, given the circumstances and what Healey and Andy Burnham are saying, it seems very unlikely that welfare spending will fall this parliament. The press release headline is a bit misleading because it implies Healey has actually ruled that out as an option.
Councils complain they've been left 'frustrated' as latest local government reorganisation update leaves many still in limbo
Patrick Butler
Patrick Butler is the Guardian’s social policy editor.
One of the government’s arguably most unloved policies – the biggest reform of local government for 50 years – continues to stumble on, with few signs that the rancour and confusion surrounding the project is dissipating.
The process started nearly two years ago, with proposals to abolish the current two-tier system of districts and counties in favour of a smaller number of unitary authorities – or “mega-councils” – covering large areas.
Plans juddered to a temporary halt in September amid legal challenges from several councils, including Reform-led Kent, Essex, and Lancashire. Ministers said a short internal review was needed to reassess merger decisions.
The outcome of that review was announced today. (See 3.20pm.) Local government minister Jim McMahon said merger decisions already made in 13 areas would be withdrawn and “reconsidered” – plunging the project into another period of uncertainty. There are another two areas were decisions are still being awaited.
The frustration across local government, which has never shown huge appetite for what it sees as a costly and time-intensive reorganisation agenda, was palpable.
Jonathan Carr West of the Local Government Information Unit said:
Councils in all of those 15 areas have put serious time, money and goodwill into this process, at government’s urging. All that effort feels in jeopardy … That is a fragile basis for a national reform programme.
Ministers insist that withdrawing those decisions does not mean the process has been abandoned. It says fresh decisions will have been made by early next year in all areas, and the new councils will be up and running by 2029.
But many councils remain unconvinced. Richard Wright, chair of the Local Councils Network, said:
Unfortunately, with some councils threatening legal challenges, even final decisions from government may not be the end of the process, so uncertainty is likely to continue for a while.
And Eamonn O’Brien, chair of the Local Government Association, said:
While today’s announcement provides some certainty for some areas, many councils remain frustrated by the situation they have been placed in. All councils affected need urgent clarity on next steps and how costs already incurred will be met.
Shadow communities secretary Katie Lam branded the government’s approach to local reorganisation “nothing short of a farce” and “a complete joke”.
Areas where plans will be reconsidered are: Derbyshire and Derby; Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Kent and Medway; Lancashire, Blackburn with Darwen and Blackpool; Leicestershire, Leicester, and Rutland; Lincolnshire, North Lincolnshire and North East Lincolnshire; Nottinghamshire and Nottingham; Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent; Essex, Southend on Sea and Thurrock; Hampshire, Isle of Wight, Portsmouth and Southampton; Norfolk; Suffolk.
Areas where reorganisation is going ahead: Surrey; East Sussex and Brighton and Hove; GLoucestershire; Oxfordshire; Warwickshire; Worcestershire.
Decisions are awaited in: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough; West Sussex.
NI's first minister says she's been blocked from summit with PM after Drumcree row provokes DUP into using veto
Andy Burnham is chairing a national economic council in Glasgow tomorrow. Ministers from the Scottish and Welsh governments will be there, but the Northern Ireland executive will not be represented because of an increasingly acrimonious dispute between Sinn Féin and the DUP.
Emma Little-Pengelly, the DUP deputy first minister, has in effect blocked Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minster, from attending. Under the power-sharing arrangements that apply at Stormont, designed to ensure unionists and nationalists have to govern together, the FM and deputy FM have equal status and Little-Pengelly has exercised her veto over their attendance at the meeting in Glasgow.
In response, O’Neill posted this on social media, accusing Little-Pengelly of a “reactive stunt”.
But Little-Pengelly defended her action, which relates to unionists being furious with O’Neill for supporting the Garvaghy Road residents who blocked an Orange Order parade at Drumcree that had been allowed by the Parades Commission. O’Neill was siding with nationalists objecting to a parade they find intimidating, but unionists argue that she should not have backed an unlawful protest.
The situation surrounding the first minister’s recent conduct remains extremely serious. There is significant anger, hurt and legitimate public discontent arising from her actions. These concerns cannot simply be dismissed or minimised. This is an exceptionally serious matter, particularly given the responsibilities of the office she holds and the importance of public confidence in the rule of law.
Of further concern is the first minister’s continuing refusal to recognise or meaningfully acknowledge the depth and legitimacy of the discontent caused by her behaviour. Her approach has contributed to a significant deterioration in confidence and in the working relationship necessary to discharge the responsibilities of our joint office.
At a news conference today, Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, backed Little-Pengelly. He said her move showed O’Neill that “law breaking must have consequences”.
Relations between Sinn Féin and the DUP were already extremely strained before Drumcree – seven months into the financial year, the executive still has not passed a budget – and this latest development shows how they are getting ever closer to collapsing entirely.
Nigel Farage accused of shoving female Lib Dem MP in parliament
Nigel Farage has been accused of having shoved a female Liberal Democrat MP earlier this year, after he spoke about missing this week’s budget because of a previous altercation about seating. Rowena Mason has the story.
Tories dismiss Labour's local government reorganisation as 'nothing short of farce' as 15 areas remain subject to review
The Conservatives have branded the Labour’s local government reorganisation programme “nothing short of a farce”. Speaking in the Commons in response to Jim McMahon’s statement saying some reorganisation projects are going ahead, while 15 are still being reviewed (see 3.20pm), Katie Lam, the shadow communities secretary, said:
It gives me no pleasure whatsoever to say that from start to finish, this government’s approach to local government reorganisation has been nothing short of a farce …
The vast majority of councils are none the wiser after what we have heard today … People across the country are left without any sense of which council will be providing services in the year and years to come, while councillors and council officials have spent millions of pounds of taxpayers’ money planning and preparing for new authorities, which may never materialise.
The money spent on this farcical reorganisation process should have been spent instead on resurfacing roads, collecting bins, and maintaining parks, local government functions that people actually care about.
For all the prime minister’s talk about local government, this whole approach to devolution has shown nothing but contempt for local democracy.
Five counties have had local government reorganisation plans confirmed, MPs told, as others still subject to review
Five counties have had their local government reorganisation plans confirmed, as officials said all regions in England would have final decisions by next year, the Press Assocation reports. PA says:
In a Commons statement, local government minister Jim McMahon said ministers had found the original criteria for the reorganisations was “robust”, after they were reviewed when Andy Burnham became PM.
The changes are part of the government’s flagship local government policy announced by Keir Starmer’s government.
It aims to replace existing two-tier systems of councils with one unitary body that will look after all local services, to streamline decision-making.
The previous proposals were announced by former communities secretary Steve Reed earlier this year, but reviewed by Labour in September.
Eamonn O’Brien, chair of the Local Government Association, said councils were “frustrated” by the process and needed “urgently clarity”.
The five areas where the government is minded to proceed are:
-In East Sussex and Brighton and Hove, the two unitary proposal including boundary changes requested by Brighton and Hove City Council, except for the parish of Falmer.
-The one unitary proposal in Gloucestershire;
-The three unitary proposal in Oxfordshire, including boundary changes.
-The two unitary proposal in Warwickshire;
-The two unitary proposal in Worcestershire.
In another 15 areas, plans are still being reviewed.
Healey says he does not accept joining EU single market would automatically be good for growth
John Healey did not just sound sceptical about rejoining the single market, or the EU proper, in his GB News interview. (See 12.14pm.) In an interview with LBC, he said that he did not accept the growth would automatically be better if the UK were in the single market.
Asked by the presenter, Nick Ferrari, if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU, or the single market, Healey replied:
Well, I don’t actually accept that.
Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union.
The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient. It’s confounded the forecasters.
When it was put to him that being in the single market could boost GDP by 4-5%, Healey said:
Well, that’s part of a bigger conversation that the prime minister wants the country to have because he recognises - and everybody, many other people do – that our Brexit deal was not a good one. It’s not been good for Britain over the last decade.
But my job now is to make sure, when you’re talking about growth, is to try and reinforce that resilience in the British economy.
Most economists believe being in the single market would boost UK growth significantly. But it would also involve aligning with EU regulations and allowing free movement, which Brexiters view as politically unacceptable.
Burnham insists letter telling ministers not to argue for specific UK-EU renegotiation outcomes doesn't mean they're gagged
Andy Burnham has rejected claims that he has stopped ministers speaking out about his plans for a closer relationship with Europe.
As mentioned earlier (see 12.14pm), Burnham wrote to ministers yesterday saying he does not want them to “advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process” as he opens a debate on forming a closer relationship with the EU. At GB News, this has been written up under the headline: “Andy Burnham gags Cabinet on rejoin EU plot”.
Asked if he was preventing ministers from speaking out in his pooled interview with broadcasters today, Burnham replied:
Not in the slightest. I have been working with the cabinet on the approach that we’re taking to Europe, and we have a clear approach now as we go into the next UK-EU summit, which is three weeks away.
For the record, this is what Burnham said in the letter sent to cabinet ministers yesterday.
I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain. It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration.
It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.
Burnham said that at the UK-EU summit on 20 November he wanted to lock in deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. But he said he would also set out the next steps for considering the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU. He went on:
Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.
I am also clear that any fundamental change to the direction of the relationship would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament.
Burnham said there was an “agreed mandate” in government for the summit. He went on:
In the period beyond the summit, government policy will be to explore options for the long-term relationship with the EU for consideration in the next parliament.
At the end of this process, we will set out to the country the respective merits and drawbacks of the various options.
It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period.
It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.
Burnham says he's confident economy will go 'from strength to strength'
Andy Burnham has claimed that the British economy is going “from strength to strength”.
Economists have argued that the documents published alongside the budget suggest this parliament will be dire for living standards. (See 10.21am.) But, asked about the country’s economic prospects when speaking to reporters on a visit in Derby, Burnham said:
The British economy is defying the expectations of forecasters, so this year we will grow more strongly. The growth forecast has been upgraded.
The IMF [International Monetary Fund] said last week we’re the standout nation for deficit reduction, so it remains difficult because the world is difficult and the situation in the Middle East has an impact.
But I think people should look at what the chancellor said yesterday, see a country that has got a platform of stability in the economy. We’re beginning to defy those expectations, and I’m confident that we will go from strength to strength from here.
Burnham claims government working 'flat out' to cut welfare spending
Andy Burnham has said the government is working ‘‘flat out” to cut welfare spending.
Speaking to reporters at a Rolls-Royce factory in Derby, when asked if he could confirm what John Healey was reported to have said about planning to cut welfare spending by the next election, Burnham replied:
We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we’re working flat out to that end. Now that we are through the budget, the big next priority in front of us is the publication of the [Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment], long awaited, but it’s coming soon.
We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There’s no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible.
Burnham also argued that “crude cuts” on their own would just leave people “in crisis”, requiring more public spending down the line.
At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was also asked if John Healey’s comments about the EU in a GB interview this morning (see 12.14pm) were out of line with Andy Burnham’s. No, was the answer. The spokesperson said:
The position of the government, and the prime minister and the chancellor, is that a stronger relationship with our closest neighbours is in our national interest.
Healey did not say anything that contradicted Burnham’s views on Brexit. But if Burnham had been asked the GB News questions, he would have stressed the problems with the current EU relationship. Healey, instead, said “we’ve got a Brexit decision” and stressed the importance of making the best of the current arrangements.
No 10 confirms government not setting timetable for when it will cut welfare spending
Downing Street has said John Healey was not committing to cutting welfare spending before the general election in his Today programme interview this morning. (See 9.23am.)
Although one answer he gave to a question could be interpreted as saying that, the PM’s spokesperson said that was not Healey’s message. The spokesperson said:
We’ve never set an arbitrary target or timetable [for when the welfare bill starts to fall]. But both the prime minister and the chancellor have been crystal clear that the welfare bill needs to come down, and that we need to do that in a progressive and sustainable way and not through crude cuts which push people into hardship and puts pressure on the system elsewhere.
Asked if Healey mis-spoke in his interview, the spokesperson said:
The chancellor is completely in line with what the PM has said over the last few months that the welfare bill needs to come down and, as I say, we are not setting an arbitrary target or timetable on that.
The spokesperson said the government would be publishing Alan Milburn’s report on youth unemployment and Stephen Timms’ report on the personal independence payment (Pip), and that these would be followed by a white paper on welfare reform published next year. That will be followed by legislation.
Badenoch claims it's 'astounding' Healey won't commit to cutting welfare bill before general election
Kemi Badenoch has described the Treasury clarification that John Healey is not promising to cut the welfare bill before the general election (see 9.23am) as “astounding”. In a response on social media, she said:
This is astounding. The government’s own figures show working-age welfare will go up by £60 BILLION by 2030, yet the Treasury has to rush out and correct the Chancellor to say there is no timetable for cutting the benefits bill. Looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading.
John Healey couldn’t even find £10 billion to get defence spending to 3% of GDP - the thing he quit over.
Don’t let anyone tell you this was a ‘do no harm budget’. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they’ve harmed our national security.

Healey (66) says he does not expect UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime

I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that …
I expect, and my job is to try and make the most of Britain’s position now.
Healey confirms government not committed to bring down welfare bill before next election

He did so in an interview with Channel 4 News, revising a message he gave out with an ambiguous answer in an interview with the Today programme. (See 9.23am.)
Asked if he was committed to reducing the welfare bill this parliament, he replied:
We’re certainly committed to bringing the cost of the welfare bill down. I’ve said that, the prime minister’s said that. It is not correct to say that we set any schedule or time limit for that.
Asked if that meant it would not come down this parliament, he replied:
It’s not correct to say that we’re going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.
Channel 4 News sent out a press release with the transcript headlined: “John Healey tells Krishnan Guru-Murthy Labour will not bring welfare bill down in this Parliament”. Healey’s not having much luck with media today because this does not seem 100% accurate either. He is saying the government has not committed to bringing the welfare bill down this parliament. But that is not the same as saying the government has committed to not bringing it down. In practice, given the circumstances and what Healey and Andy Burnham are saying, it seems very unlikely that welfare spending will fall this parliament. The press release headline is a bit misleading because it implies Healey has actually ruled that out as an option.

The IMF [International Monetary Fund] said last week we’re the standout nation for deficit reduction, so it remains difficult because the world is difficult and the situation in the Middle East has an impact.
But I think people should look at what the chancellor said yesterday, see a country that has got a platform of stability in the economy. We’re beginning to defy those expectations, and I’m confident that we will go from strength to strength from here.
Burnham claims government working 'flat out' to cut welfare spending
Andy Burnham has said the government is working ‘‘flat out” to cut welfare spending.
Speaking to reporters at a Rolls-Royce factory in Derby, when asked if he could confirm what John Healey was reported to have said about planning to cut welfare spending by the next election, Burnham replied:
We want to get the welfare bill down as quickly as possible, and we’re working flat out to that end. Now that we are through the budget, the big next priority in front of us is the publication of the [Alan Milburn report on youth unemployment], long awaited, but it’s coming soon.
We just want to get stuck into supporting people to help people off benefits and into work. There’s no delay there. We want that to happen as quickly as possible.
Burnham also argued that “crude cuts” on their own would just leave people “in crisis”, requiring more public spending down the line.
At the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson was also asked if John Healey’s comments about the EU in a GB interview this morning (see 12.14pm) were out of line with Andy Burnham’s. No, was the answer. The spokesperson said:
The position of the government, and the prime minister and the chancellor, is that a stronger relationship with our closest neighbours is in our national interest.
Healey did not say anything that contradicted Burnham’s views on Brexit. But if Burnham had been asked the GB News questions, he would have stressed the problems with the current EU relationship. Healey, instead, said “we’ve got a Brexit decision” and stressed the importance of making the best of the current arrangements.
No 10 confirms government not setting timetable for when it will cut welfare spending
Downing Street has said John Healey was not committing to cutting welfare spending before the general election in his Today programme interview this morning. (See 9.23am.)
Although one answer he gave to a question could be interpreted as saying that, the PM’s spokesperson said that was not Healey’s message. The spokesperson said:
We’ve never set an arbitrary target or timetable [for when the welfare bill starts to fall]. But both the prime minister and the chancellor have been crystal clear that the welfare bill needs to come down, and that we need to do that in a progressive and sustainable way and not through crude cuts which push people into hardship and puts pressure on the system elsewhere.
Asked if Healey mis-spoke in his interview, the spokesperson said:
The chancellor is completely in line with what the PM has said over the last few months that the welfare bill needs to come down and, as I say, we are not setting an arbitrary target or timetable on that.
The spokesperson said the government would be publishing Alan Milburn’s report on youth unemployment and Stephen Timms’ report on the personal independence payment (Pip), and that these would be followed by a white paper on welfare reform published next year. That will be followed by legislation.
Badenoch claims it's 'astounding' Healey won't commit to cutting welfare bill before general election
Kemi Badenoch has described the Treasury clarification that John Healey is not promising to cut the welfare bill before the general election (see 9.23am) as “astounding”. In a response on social media, she said:
This is astounding. The government’s own figures show working-age welfare will go up by £60 BILLION by 2030, yet the Treasury has to rush out and correct the Chancellor to say there is no timetable for cutting the benefits bill. Looks like foot in mouth syndrome is spreading.
John Healey couldn’t even find £10 billion to get defence spending to 3% of GDP - the thing he quit over.
Don’t let anyone tell you this was a ‘do no harm budget’. In doing so little, Labour have harmed our economic security and they’ve harmed our national security.

title: Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
content_c:
Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
October 30, 2026
The German pharmaceutical giant Bayer won a trial on Thursday over claims the Roundup weedkiller, manufactured by subsidiary Monsanto, caused cancer in three women.
The Missouri jury sided unanimously with Bayer. It's the first trial since a US Supreme Court ruling that limits complaints over the product.
Bayer is waiting for a separate court ruling where the company is seeking a $7.25 billion (€6.5 billion) settlement in relation to tens of thousands of other Roundup cases.
What is the complaint against Roundup?
Thursday's court ruling follows a case brought to a St. Louis court by Theresa Aretino, Cynthia Fernandez and Betty Larkin in 2020.
The three women had said they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after regularly using the weedkiller.
Their attorneys argued that Roundup was defectively designed and unreasonably dangerous, and that Bayer was negligent in selling it.
The three were not participating in the Bayer settlement. Some 65,000 other cases have been filed against the company, claiming Roundup gave them cancer.
What did the Supreme Court rule in regards to Roundup?
The US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that plaintiffs could not argue that the Roundup label failed to warn users about the risk of cancer since the US Environmental Protection Agency had concluded the label does not require a cancer warning.
"We are pleased with the jury's favorable verdict for Monsanto validating our belief that there is no evidence to prove design defect, fraud or negligence claims in the Roundup litigation," Bill Dodero, the company's US general counsel and global head of litigation, said in a statement.
"This verdict should send a strong signal that plaintiffs who wish to pursue claims in the court system following the Durnell ruling will face significant challenges both in demonstrating they have viable claims and putting forth the necessary evidence to prove them in court," he added, using the name of the Supreme Court case.
The company has repeatedly defended the use of glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, as safe, calling it "one of the most studied agricultural tools in history."
The EPA has previously concluded that glyphosate is probably not carcinogenic, but it is in the middle of a new review of its safety. The International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2015 that the chemical was "probably carcinogenic" to humans, but Bayer has rejected the study's findings, calling it an outlier.

title: News: EU-Kanada-Gipfel, Interview mit Anthony Scaramucci, Deutsch-Türkisches Anwerbeabkommen
content_c:
Die Lage am Morgen »Kartoffel. Ich liebe Dich!«
- Warum Kanada nun doch kein assoziiertes EU-Mitglied wird – und was Friedrich Merz damit zu tun hat
- Was der ehemalige Trump-Kommunikator Anthony Scaramucci über seinen Ex-Chef zu sagen hat – und warum ein Pferd kein Zebra ist
- Wie aus Gastarbeitern Kolleginnen, Nachbarn und Freunde wurden – und wie mutig die frühen türkischen Einwanderinnen waren
Kanada bleibt fernes Land
Ursula von der Leyen wollte ihren Verhandlungspartnern in Montreal eine assoziierte EU-Mitgliedschaft anbieten, aber, halten Sie sich fest, es war leider Kanada. Bitte verzeihen Sie den kleinen Flachwitz, er hat immerhin einen realen Hintergrund: Denn ähnlich flach fällt heute die Abschlusserklärung des EU-Kanada-Gipfels aus, auf dem von der Leyen eigentlich ihre vollmundige Ankündigung vom September vorantreiben wollte, Kanada zum assoziierten EU-Mitglied zu machen (mehr dazu hier).
Wobei niemand so genau sagen konnte, was das eigentlich konkret bedeuten sollte. In der Abschlusserklärung soll jetzt nur noch von einer »Allianz für die Zukunft« die Rede sein.
EU-Kommissionschefin Ursula von der Leyen in Montreal (29. Oktober 2026)
Foto: Graham Hughes / EPA
Über den Grund dafür berichten meine Kollegen Timo Lehmann und Benedikt Müller-Arnold: Von der Leyens Vorschlag stieß auf den Widerstand von Friedrich Merz. Der hatte nämlich zuvor eigene Assoziationspläne für die Ukraine geäußert (mehr dazu hier), das allein wäre schon kompliziert genug. Und dann auch noch ein Sonderstatus für ein zweites Land, unter vollkommen anderen Voraussetzungen? Der Vorstoß der umtriebigen EU-Kommissionschefin passte nicht zu Merz’ Agenda.
Kritiker werfen von der Leyen nun vor, dass sie sich nicht ausreichend mit den EU-Mitgliedstaaten abgestimmt habe. Und sie bemängeln, dass in Europa über Begriffe gestritten wird, statt die Partnerschaft mit Kanada auf den Weg zu bringen. So wird eine hoffnungsvolle Idee zum traurigen Witz.
- Die ganze Geschichte hier: Warum der Kanzler von der Leyens Kanada-Plan durchkreuzte
Ein Pferd ist kein Zebra
In den USA stehen die Midterms bevor, die wichtigen Zwischenwahlen. Während wir darauf warten, dass die Amerikaner Donald Trump zur lahmen Ente ohne Mehrheit in Repräsentantenhaus und Senat wählen, vertreiben wir uns die Zeit mit einem unterhaltsamen Blick auf die US-Politik. Und wohl kaum jemand spricht farbenfroher als Anthony Scaramucci.
»The Mooch«, der Schnorrer, wie er auch genannt wird, war in der ersten Amtszeit Trumps einmal für elf Tage der Kommunikationschef des Weißen Hauses. Er hat es sich in dieser Zeit aber so rapide mit den anderen Getreuen des Präsidenten verdorben, dass Trump ihn schnell fallen ließ (mehr dazu hier). Seither ist Scaramucci immer gut für ein saftiges Zitat gegen seinen Ex-Chef.
Ex-Trump-Sprecher Anthony Scaramucci
Foto:
Jose Sarmento Matos / Bloomberg / Getty Images
Hier ein paar Kostproben des Gesprächs, das meine Kollegin Britta Kollenbroich und mein Kollege Maximilian Popp mit Scaramucci geführt haben: Wie erklärt er sich Trumps Nähe zu Putin? »Wenn du das Fenster öffnest und das Klappern von Hufen hörst, dann ist es ein Pferd und kein Zebra. Was Trump tut, kann man nicht ohne Grund tun. Putin hat ihn wahrscheinlich unter Druck gesetzt.«
Könnte JD Vance Trump beerben? »Er hat kein Charisma. Diese Sonnenbrille in meiner Tasche hat mehr Charisma.« Kann Trump die Stimmung vor den Wahlen noch drehen? »Wir wissen, dass Trump bei Wahlen besser abschneidet als in Umfragen.« Ob die Einschätzungen Scaramuccis mehr Gewicht haben als seine Sonnenbrille? Nächste Woche wissen wir mehr.
- Das ganze Interview hier: »Trump ist müde. Daran gibt es keinen Zweifel. Aber unterschätzt ihn nicht«
Schön, dass Ihr da seid
Als die Schneiderin Sümer Hanım am Gleis 11 auf dem Münchner Hauptbahnhof aus dem Zug stieg, hatte sie eine 50 Stunden lange Fahrt von Istanbul nach München hinter sich. Ihre beiden kleinen Töchter musste die geschiedene 30-Jährige zunächst in der Türkei zurücklassen, sie wollte sie möglichst bald nachholen. Jetzt aber machte sie sich erst einmal auf die Suche nach einem neuen Leben in einem fremden Land. Gefragt, ob sie Deutsch spreche, antwortete sie mit den einzigen Wörtern, die sie damals kannte: »Kartoffel. Ich liebe Dich!«
Autorin Gün Tank
Foto: Marlena Waldthausen / DER SPIEGEL
Diese Geschichte steht auf einer Tafel am Münchner Hauptbahnhof. Angebracht wurde sie zum Gedenken an das deutsch-türkische Anwerbeabkommen aus dem Jahr 1961. Die Bundesrepublik brauchte Arbeitskräfte, und es kamen Menschen.
Heute, am 65. Jahrestag der Unterzeichnung des Abkommens, leben rund 2,6 Millionen Menschen mit türkischer Einwanderungsgeschichte in Deutschland – also solche, die entweder selbst eingewandert sind oder deren beide Eltern aus der Türkei kamen. Längst sind das keine sogenannten Gastarbeiter mehr, sondern Kolleginnen und Kollegen, Nachbarn und Freunde, die ganz selbstverständlich dazugehören.
Im Interview mit meiner Kollegin Fiona Ehlers erinnert die Autorin Gün Tank vor allem an die mutigen Frauen, die sich damals auf den Weg nach Deutschland gemacht haben: »Angeworben wurden sie als billige und fingerfertige Arbeitskräfte, man hielt sie für leicht lenkbar. Doch bald begannen sie, für ihre Rechte zu kämpfen, organisierten sich und streikten für gleichen Lohn. Diese Haltung beeindruckt mich noch heute.«
- Das ganze Interview hier: »Ihre ersten Worte lauteten: Schnell, schnell, Akkord, Akkord«
Hier geht’s zum aktuellen Tagesquiz
Noch mehr Rätsel wie Viererkette, Wordle und Paarsuche finden Sie bei SPIEGEL Games.
Verlierer des Tages …
Sir Patrick Stewart (1940 – 2026)
Foto: Paul Buck / EPA
… sind heute die Star Trek-Fans dieser Welt, denn sie haben ihren weisen Captain Jean-Luc Picard verloren: Gestern Abend wurde bekannt, dass der britische Schauspieler Sir Patrick Stewart am Mittwoch im Alter von 86 Jahren gestorben ist.
- Die ganze Nachricht hier: Patrick Stewart ist tot
Die jüngsten Meldungen aus der Nacht
- US-Justizministerium erhöht vor Midterms Druck auf Kalifornien: Donald Trump behauptet seit Langem, dass Nicht-Staatsbürger in großem Stil an US-Wahlen teilnehmen. Die Regierung hat Medienbericht zufolge nun Vorladungen an Wahlbeamte in Kalifornien verschickt – wenige Tage vor den Zwischenwahlen.
- Eisenkot wirft Netanyahu vor, er wolle Israels Wahlergebnis »delegitimieren«: Benjamin Netanyahu hat keine Mehrheit mehr in der Knesset. Seine Likud-Partei bezeichnete die Wahl prompt als »gestohlen«. Oppositionsführer Gadi Eisenkot reagierte mit deutlichen Worten.
- Vereinigte Staaten sollen Audi zehn Prozent Zoll für Einfuhren angeboten haben: Für Autos aus Europa kassieren die USA 15 Prozent Einfuhrzoll, aus Mexiko sogar 25 Prozent. Audi soll künftig deutlich weniger zahlen – als Gegenleistung für den geplanten Fabrikneubau in Georgia.
Heute bei SPIEGEL Extra: Wie macht man den besten Kartoffelbrei?
[M] DER SPIEGEL; Fotos: Maximilian Probst / DER SPIEGEL, vikif / iStockphoto / Getty Images
Was ist das Geheimnis von Kartoffelpüree? Das wollten Sie von unserem SPIEGEL-Küchenkabinett wissen. Hier erklären unsere drei Profis, wie Sie den perfekten Stampf zubereiten .
Ich wünsche Ihnen einen guten Start in den Tag.
Ihr Stefan Kuzmany, Autor der Chefredaktion

title: Frankreich bereitet sich auf neue Schülerproteste vor
content_c:
Schülerproteste in Frankreich "Was wir bekommen haben, sind bloß Krümel"
Frankreich stellt sich auf ein unruhiges Wochenende ein: Erneut wollen Schüler im ganzen Land gegen die Bildungspolitik protestieren. Denn die ersten Zugeständnisse der Regierung reichen ihnen nicht aus.
Die Behörden werden alles tun, damit die bevorstehende Halloween-Nacht nicht zum Horror wird. Schon Anfang der Woche warnte Präsident Macron: "C’est un samedi à risque." - Der nächste Samstag werde wieder risikoreich. Denn die Schülerinnen und Schüler wollen erneut auf die Straße gehen.
Zwar haben sie den Fünf-Punkte-Plan des Bildungsministers Geffray begrüßt. Dieser hatte am Dienstag zugesagt, die Klassenstärke zu reduzieren, 500 zusätzliche Lehrerstellen zu schaffen, vergünstigte Kredite im Umfang von vier Milliarden Euro für die Renovierung der Schulgebäude zur Verfügung zu stellen und das umstrittene System zur Studienplatzvergabe zu reformieren. Doch unterm Strich reichen den Schülern die Ankündigungen nicht.
Für den französischen Innenminister Laurent Nuñez gibt es deswegen ein "sehr hohes Risiko urbaner Gewalt". Demonstrationen in den Stadtzentren würden nicht erlaubt. Gegen Gewalt und Plünderungen werde die Polizei mit "äußerster Entschlossenheit" vorgehen.
In ganz Frankreich werden am Samstag wie am vergangenen Wochenende 70.000 Polizisten im Einsatz sein. Der französische Innenminister erwartet ähnlich viele Demonstranten wie vor einer Woche, als über 400.000 Menschen in Frankreich überwiegend friedlich demonstriert haben.
Macron kritisiert hohe Forderungen
"Was wir bekommen haben, sind bloß Krümel angesichts dessen, was wir gefordert haben", bemängelte Schülersprecher Clement Vieillot. "Wir wollen 250.000 neue Studienplätze und sie haben nur 15.000 neue Plätze bewilligt." Sein Mitstreiter Marius Mesnil von der Schülergewerkschaft Union Syndicale Lycéenne fügte hinzu: "Das ist zu wenig: Wir fordern 250.000 neue Studienplätze, damit keine Bewerber mehr aussortiert werden."
Präsident Macron warnte vor maximalistischen Forderungen. Im Gespräch mit dem Youtuber Hugo Décrypte erklärte er, dass er in den letzten zehn Jahren 500.000 neue Studienplätze geschaffen habe und betonte: "In unserem Land ist das Studium kostenlos." Auch die Studierendenversicherung sei inzwischen kostenlos und die Stipendien erhöht worden.
"Wir müssen mit der Idee Schluss machen, es gäbe ein universelles Recht auf ein Universitätsstudium. Das sei "falsch und auch nicht wünschenswert", so Macron.
Regierung hofft auf erneuten Präsenzunterricht
Doch vielen Schülerinnen und Schülern ist der Druck zu groß. Sie prangern die Konkurrenz bei der Studienplatzvergabe an und wollen erreichen, dass in den letzten zwei Schuljahren nicht mehr alle Noten aus den Schwerpunktfächern fürs Abitur zählen. Zudem kritisieren sie die langen Schultage und die Benachteiligung von Schülern aus den Banlieues, also den Randgebieten großer Städte, und den Übersee-Departements.
Die Regierung räumte ein, zu spät reagiert zu haben, hofft nun aber, dass nach den Herbstferien wieder Präsenzunterricht stattfinden kann. "Das ist entscheidend, gerade für die Studienanfänger", sagte Hochschulminister Philippe Batiste gegenüber dem Sender France Info.
"Fast die Hälfte von ihnen bricht nach einem Jahr ab und jetzt haben sie seit dem Studienstart Anfang September nur drei bis vier Wochen Unterricht gehabt." So riskiere Frankreich "im übertragenen Sinne ein Massensterben an der Uni". Präsenzunterricht bedeute ja nicht, dass die Demonstrierenden ihre Forderungen aufgeben müssten, betonte Batiste.
Das haben sie auch nicht vor. Im Gegenteil: Am Samstag wollen sie gemeinsam mit den Gelbwesten und Gewerkschaften erneut auf die Straße gehen.

title: Kampf den Schattenflotten: Was kann die EU ohne die USA tun?
content_c:
Kampf den Schattenflotten: Was kann die EU ohne die USA tun?
29. Oktober 2026
Seit Russlands Überfall auf die Ukraine setzt Moskau verstärkt auf eine sogenannte Schattenflotte, um westliche Sanktionen zu umgehen und sein Öl weltweit exportieren zu können. Auch andere Länder, die mit starken Sanktionen belegt sind, darunter Iran und Venezuela, werden beschuldigt, solche Schiffe für den Export von Erdölprodukten zu nutzen.
Diese Tanker greifen häufig auf Täuschungsmanöver zurück, wie beispielsweise das Abschalten ihrer Ortungssender, um der Entdeckung zu entgehen und die wahren Herkunfts- oder Bestimmungsorte der Ladung zu verschleiern.
Die Flotten, die größtenteils aus veralteten, nicht versicherten und schlecht gewarteten Tankern bestehen, lösen in der Schifffahrtsbranche große Besorgnis aus. Dennoch sind sie in den letzten Jahren rasant gewachsen und macht Schätzungen des Finanzinformationsunternehmens S&P Global zufolge mittlerweile fast 19 Prozent der globalen Öltankerkapazität aus.
"Die Schattenflotte ist eine Geißel", sagte Elisabeth Braw, Senior Fellow beim Thinktank Atlantic Council, und fügte hinzu: Es liege "in niemandes Interesse", dass diese Schiffe auf den Weltmeeren unterwegs sind. Sie wies darauf hin, dass diese Tanker die maritime Ordnung untergraben und das Risiko von Unfällen und Umweltschäden erhöhen. "Jedes Land sollte seinen Einfluss auf Russland nutzen, um es aufzufordern, die Flotte nicht einzusetzen", sagte sie gegenüber der DW und merkte an, dass letztendlich alle Länder die Folgen tragen.
Lockerung der Sanktionen?
Um die Flotte einzudämmen und Russlands Ölexporterlöse zu dämpfen, haben die Vereinigten Staaten und europäische Länder ihre Bemühungen verstärkt, Tanker abzufangen, die der Verletzung von Sanktionen beschuldigt werden. Die Trump-Regierung erwägt jedoch Berichten zufolge, die Sanktionen gegen einige Schiffe der Schattenflotte aufzuheben und ihnen den Transport von Öl zu erlauben, das nicht den Sanktionen unterliegt.
Ein US-Beamter sagte Reuters Anfang des Monats, dass dieser Schritt darauf abziele, die rekordhohen globalen Frachtraten zu senken. Die Aufhebung der Sanktionen gegen die Schattenflotte "würde die Wirksamkeit des Sanktionsregimes insgesamt verringern", sagte Michael Carpenter, Senior Fellow für transatlantische Angelegenheiten am International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS). Ein solcher Schritt "belohnt den Aggressor und hilft Moskau, Einnahmen zu generieren, um die Angriffe auf die Ukraine fortzusetzen", sagte er gegenüber der DW. "Das ist genau das Gegenteil von dem, was die USA tun sollten, wenn sie den Krieg beenden wollen."
Carpenter, der zuvor als US-Botschafter bei der Organisation für Sicherheit und Zusammenarbeit in Europa (OSZE) tätig war, sagte, jede Lockerung der Sanktionen würde die USA und die EU "strategisch gegeneinander ausspielen, wobei die EU die Ukraine klar unterstützt und die USA zunehmend Russlands finanzielle Ziele fördern."
Diese Ansicht teilt auch Ben Harris, Vizepräsident und Direktor für Wirtschaftsstudien an der Brookings Institution. Die Aufhebung der Sanktionen gegen Tanker der Schattenflotte würde es Russland "erheblich erleichtern, sein Öl zu Marktpreisen zu handeln", sagte er und wies darauf hin, dass dies "die Staatsfinanzen verbessern würde, da ein Großteil der Einnahmen an die Energiemärkte gekoppelt ist."
US-Energieminister Chris Wright wies jedoch Vermutungen zurück, die USA würden die Sanktionen gegen Tanker der Schattenflotte aufheben. "Wir wandeln Schattentanker in legale Tanker um", zitierte Bloomberg Wright letzte Woche. "Die Sanktionen werden nicht aufgehoben", betonte er und fügte hinzu, die US-Regierung arbeite mit Investoren zusammen, die stillgelegte, sanktionierte Tanker kaufen, sie modernisieren und für den Transport von nicht sanktioniertem Öl einsetzen.
"Wir werden einige Schiffe aus der sogenannten 'Bösewicht-Flotte' in die 'Gute-Flotte' umsetzen", sagte Wright. "Sie werden kein sanktioniertes Öl mehr transportieren." Die US-Regierung hat noch keinen detaillierten Plan für die Schattenflotte vorgelegt.
Was haben Trump und Putin vor?
Der Vorschlag folgt einem Abkommen, das US-Präsident Donald Trump diesen Monat mit seinem russischen Amtskollegen Wladimir Putin geschlossen hat, um den Verkauf von russischem Diesel auf den Weltmärkten zu ermöglichen. Das Abkommen wurde als Teil von Trumps Bemühungen gesehen, die Kraftstoffpreise im Inland vor den US-Zwischenwahlen am 3. November zu senken.
Der US-Präsident setzte außerdem weitreichende neue Sanktionen gegen Russland aus, die durch ein kürzlich verabschiedetes Gesetz autorisiert worden waren und Moskaus Energieeinnahmen betrafen sowie Zölle gegen die weltweit größten Abnehmer von russischem Öl und Gas androhten.
Die Entscheidung wurde von der Ukraine und ihren europäischen Verbündeten scharf kritisiert, da sie befürchteten, sie könne die Glaubwürdigkeit der Sanktionen untergraben und den westlichen Wirtschaftsdruck auf Moskau schwächen. Harris sagte: "Die US-Sanktionen haben ein überproportionales Gewicht, weil sie die Gefahr bergen, dass Länder und Unternehmen vom US-Finanzsystem abgeschnitten werden."
Was kann die EU tun?
Sollten die USA ihre Sanktionen gegen die Schattenflotte aufgeben, argumentierte er, "verlagert sich die Verantwortung auf die europäischen Entscheidungsträger". Allerdings stünden ihnen "weniger wirksame Optionen zur Verfügung, da die Gefahr eines Abbruchs der Finanzbeziehungen geringer geworden ist".
Der Experte betonte jedoch, dass Europa über einige Instrumente verfüge und verwies auf die Schlüsselrolle des Kontinents im globalen Schifffahrts- und Versicherungswesen. "Sie können Maßnahmen ergreifen, die vorschreiben, dass Tanker bei Fahrten durch ihre Gewässer eine gültige und etablierte Versicherung mitführen müssen", sagte er und merkte an, dies bedeute, "dass viele Tanker der Schattenflotte in der Praxis kein legales russisches Öl transportieren könnten".
Harris fügte hinzu, dass die europäischen Entscheidungsträger auch Druck auf Länder weltweit ausüben könnten, um die unter ihrer Flagge fahrenden Tanker besser zu regulieren. Carpenter sagte, selbst wenn Washington einige Beschränkungen lockere, bleibe der EU nichts anderes übrig, als ihre Sanktionen gegen diese Schiffe weiterhin durchzusetzen.
"Der Großteil der Schattenflotte durchquert die Ostsee und verlässt sie über die dänische Meerenge", bemerkte er und fügte hinzu, die EU sei "in einer einzigartigen Position, um Schiffe, die diesen wichtigen Engpass passieren, zu entern und zu inspizieren". Moskau drohte jedoch, Schiffe europäischer Länder zu beschlagnahmen, um sich für das Abfangen und Beschlagnahmen russischer Schiffe zu rächen, die im Verdacht stehen, Teil der Schattenflotte zu sein.
Und ohne die Unterstützung der USA, so Carpenter, "wird es für die EU-Länder schwieriger sein, die Lasten und Risiken der Sanktionsdurchsetzung zu tragen". Braw stimmte dieser Ansicht zu und sagte, die europäischen Verbündeten der Ukraine müssten zusammenhalten und weiterhin eng mit Partnern wie Japan, Australien und Kanada zusammenarbeiten. Dennoch betonte sie, dass sie allein "weit weniger erreichen können als mit der Unterstützung der USA".
Dieser Beitrag wurde aus dem Englischen adaptiert.

title: Погода у Києві 30 жовтня підготувала сюрприз: до чого готуватися жителям столиці
content_c:
Погода у Києві 30 жовтня підготувала сюрприз: до чого готуватися жителям столиці
Протягом усього дня 30 жовтня у столиці та області зберігатиметься помірне тепло без опадів, проте зі зміною напрямку вітру.
У п’ятницю, 30 жовтня, на Київщині та в столиці очікується хмарна погода з проясненнями без істотних опадів.
В Українському гідрометцентрі повідомляють, що на Київщині 30 жовтня буде хмарно із проясненнями та без істотних опадів. Вітер дутиме північно-східний та зі швидкістю 5-10 м/с.
Температура повітря по області вдень коливатиметься від +7 до +12 градусів тепла, у Києві вдень стовпчики термометрів показуватимуть близько +10.
На погодному порталі Sinoptik повідомляють, що протягом усього дня у Києві буде триматися хмарна погода. Без опадів. Температура повітря коливатиметься від +7 до +10 градусів тепла.
Раніше синоптики розповіли, якою буде погода в Україні 30 жовтня.
Підписуйтесь на наші канали у Telegram та Viber.

title: ВАКС снизил залог нескольким фигурантам дела «Карфаген», в частности Кропиве
content_c:
Высший антикоррупционный суд снизил залог трем фигурантам дела «Карфаген» о покровительстве сотрудниками генпрокуратуры колл-центров, сообщает Transparency International Ukraine. В то же время этим трем фигурантам продлили сроки содержания под стражей еще на 60 суток.
Решения касаются:
- предполагаемого организатора схемы Сергея Кропивы («Канцлера») — залог уменьшили со 120 млн грн до 93,1 млн грн;
- адвоката Александра Дидича — залог уменьшили с 15 млн грн до 11,7 млн грн;
- фигуранта без указания имени — 15 млн грн.
4 сентября НАБУ и САП объявили об операции «Карфаген» — расследовании деятельности предполагаемой преступной организации во главе с должностным лицом Офиса генерального прокурора, причастной, по версии следствия, к прикрытию мошеннических колл-центров и легализации средств.
Первым задержанным стал сотрудник ОГП Сергей Кропива — «Канцлер» в материалах НАБУ. Следственные действия проводились в служебных помещениях Офиса генпрокурора, а также у заместительницы генпрокурора Марии Вдовиченко и главы Одесской ОВА Олега Кипера, который ранее возглавлял Киевскую городскую прокуратуру.
По информации источников ZN.UA, в Украине могут действовать около двух тысяч мошеннических колл-центров. Более тысячи из них в этой среде называют «белыми». Не потому, что они работают законно, а потому, что имеют силовое прикрытие, платят ежемесячную «абонплату» и могут не опасаться обысков.
Центры, не входящие в эту систему, называют «чёрными» или «партизанами». Именно они, по словам собеседников ZN.UA, чаще всего становятся объектами показательных обысков и имитации борьбы с колл-центрами.
Непосредственно бывший генпрокурор-беглец Руслан Кравченко в деле пока не фигурирует, но на записях упоминается «Шеф», имя которого ни детектив НАБУ, ни прокурор САП пока не разглашали. Они отмечают, что «Шеф» ранее был руководителем Налоговой службы, а «Канцлер» во время телефонного разговора с одним из своих пособников называет его «Андреевичем», что совпадает с биографическими данными и отчеством действующего генерального прокурора.

title: Поліція поставила крапку у справі про смерть Панеттьєр: колишня дівчина Кличка померла випадково
content_c:
Поліція поставила крапку у справі про смерть Панеттьєр: колишня дівчина Кличка померла випадково
  - Author, Нардін Саад
  - Role, BBC News
- Published
- Час прочитання: 3 хв
Поліція Південної Кароліни повідомила, що смерть американської акторки Гейден Панеттьєр визнали випадковою. Це завершило місцеве розслідування її смерті.
Зірка серіалів "Герої" та "Нешвілл" померла у віці 36 років у серпні цього року від токсичного впливу фентанілу, ксанаксу та кількох інших препаратів, що потрапили до її організму.
Посилаючись на звіт судово-медичного експерта, в якому було встановлено, що Панеттьєр померла від передозування, поліцейське управління Грінвілла заявило, що "завершило розслідування" її смерті.
Повідомляється, що Агентство США з боротьби з наркотиками (DEA) приєдналося до місцевого поліцейського розслідування. Наразі незрозуміло, чи завершилося їхнє розслідування також. BBC звернулася до DEA за коментарем.
"На підставі висновку судово-медичного експерта та результатів розслідування смерть Гейден Панеттьєр визнано нещасним випадком", — йдеться в заяві поліції.
Зловживання наркотиками
Панеттьєр, яка відверто розповідала про свої проблеми зі зловживанням психоактивними речовинами, 16 серпня знайшли в будинку в Південній Кароліні без ознак притомності.
Минулого місяця офіс коронера округу Грінвілл підтвердив, що колишня зірка померла внаслідок випадкового передозування наркотиками, серед яких був фентаніл — синтетичний опіоїд, що лише за останні п'ять років забрав життя сотень тисяч американців.
Коронер також виявив метокарбамол, рецептурний міорелаксант, та кветіапін, антипсихотичний препарат, який застосовують для лікування певних психічних розладів.
За повідомленням офісу коронера, у акторки сталася зупинка серця, а розтин тіла не виявив жодних ознак травм, що могли б призвести до смерті.
Згідно з поліцейським звітом, складеним у день смерті, на момент прибуття екстрених служб поруч із нею перебували її колишній хлопець Браян Хікерсон (який визнав, що чинив щодо неї насильство) та його брат Зак.
Гейден Панеттьєр була колишньою нареченою українського боксера, ексчемпіона світу Володимира Кличка і матір'ю його доньки.
"Хоча Гейден більше не була моєю партнеркою, вона залишалася важливою частиною мого життя та матір'ю нашої доньки Каї", - написав він у дописі на Фейсбук.
За його словами, Панеттьєр "побудувала неймовірну кар'єру, водночас стикаючись із темними сторонами дуже вимогливої індустрії".
"Нашій доньці Каї я завжди розповідатиму про її матір із повагою і подбаю про те, щоб вона пам'ятала, якою людиною була її мама".
Володимир Кличко і Гейден Панеттьєр почали зустрічатися в 2009 році, а в 2013 році оголосили про заручини.
В 2014 році у пари народилася донька Кая-Євдокія. В 2015 році дитину охрестили в Києво-Печерській Лаврі, на церемонії був мер Києва Віталій Кличко.
Гейден разом з нареченим відвідували Київ під час Революції гідності (Євромайдану) взимку 2013-2014 років і неодноразово висловлювала підтримку українському народу.
В 2018 році стало відомо, що Володимир Кличко і Гейден Панеттьєр розійшлися, а дитина передана під опіку батька.
Зірка з пелюшок
Як розповідала сама Панеттьєр, уперше вона з'явилася на екрані у віці 11 місяців - у рекламі. Тож вже у 21 могла казати, що її акторська кар'єра триває двадцять років.
Їй було 16 років, коли в її голлівудському житті вперше з'явилися наркотики. Перед виходом на червону доріжку на честь популярного серіалу "Герої" хтось із її команди дав їй таблетку, щоб додати енергії.
Смерть Панеттьєр сталася невдовзі після виходу її мемуарів, у яких вона детально розповіла про боротьбу із залежністю, післяпологову депресію та втрату 28-річного брата.
Брат Панеттьєр, Джансен, помер у віці 28 років від серцевого захворювання. У своїй книжці вона розповіла, що перед смертю він вживав героїн і кокаїн.
Утім, у 2024, після його смерті, актриса заявила виданню People, що твердо вирішила залишатися тверезою, зазначивши, що її залежність залишилася "позаду".

title: Війська РФ атакували промислове підприємство у Кременчуцькому районі Полтавщини – ОВА
content_c:
Війська РФ у п'ятницю завдали удару по одному з промислових підприємств у Кременчуцькому районі Полтавської області, повідомив голова Полтавської обласної військової адміністрації Віталій Дяківнич у п'ятницю.
"У Кременчуцькому районі ворог атакував одне з промислових підприємств. Інформація уточнюється", – написав голова ОВА у своєму телеграм-каналі.
За словами Дяківнича, детальні дані щодо наслідків ворожого удару наразі встановлюються.
Раніше, кількість постраждалих унаслідок ворожої атаки на Кременчук Полтавської області у четвер зросла до 32 людей, серед них шестеро дітей.
Джерело: https://t.me/poltavskaOVA/35203

title: Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
content_c:
Three dead after two helicopters collide midair near Oregon airport
- Published
Three people have died after two helicopters collided midair near a small airport in Oregon, officials said.
The collision involving a Robinson R22 and an Airbus helicopter occurred near McMinnville Municipal Airport on Thursday afternoon. Both aircraft crashed in a field adjacent to a highway, the sheriff's office said.
Authorities identified the victims as a 22-year-old flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the United Kingdom, who were aboard one of the helicopters. The sole occupant of the other aircraft was also killed.
It was not immediately clear what caused the crash.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) responded to the scene and are leading the ongoing investigation.
The BBC has contacted the FAA for comment.
The flight instructor on the Robinson R22 was identified Maddie Aasbo. The student pilot from the UK has not yet been publicly identified, as authorities work with the consulate and the FBI to notify the next of kin.
The sole occupant of the Airbus was identified as Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, of Newberg, Oregon.
One of the aircraft was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training school based at the McMinnville Municipal Airport, according to a statement from the company.
"Jerry Trimble Helicopters is deeply saddened to confirm that one of our aircraft was involved in an aviation incident this afternoon," the company said, adding that they were fully cooperating with investigators.
Authorities asked the public to avoid the area as they responded to the incident.

title: 'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
content_c:
'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
- Published
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.
Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.
Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.
The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.
In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.
But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.
"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.
"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.
However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.
- Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election 
  - Published19 hours ago
- What we now know about the UK economy in four charts 
  - Published1 day ago
- Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you 
  - Published14 hours ago
In response to this "painful" situation the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.
Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains "already behind us".
Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.
The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.
Lost decade
Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.
The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.
The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.
Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.
However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.
While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.
The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.
Helen Miller, director of the influential think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the outlook was "depressing".
"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," she said.
"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."
'Fragile' finances
There would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament, Miller added.
"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.
"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.
Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.
Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.
He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.
Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.
But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" or the buffer that the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.
Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

title: Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
content_c:
Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
- Published
It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".
Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.
A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.
It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.
It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".
This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.
The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of £65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.
The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.
If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.
It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.
The detail may come more quickly than feared. On welfare, the Milburn Review process is clearly heading for some sort of welfare-to-work scheme, even a separate system for younger workers.
It will cost money up front to subsidise work opportunities and hope to save more from welfare bills in the future. The chancellor saw at close quarters Gordon Brown do this twice two decades ago.
The Office for Budget Responsbility's (OBR) economic forecast showed the sheer rise in the welfare bill, which is set to jump to £431bn in 2031, if pensioner support is included.
There are two further areas where the chancellor laid down markers, with little fiscal cost, in terms of the long term plan.
On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power.
While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.
On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected.
There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.
How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge.
Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?
Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030.
The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.
A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.
But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.
description: Chancellor John Healey's plans fall short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.

title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win
content_c:
Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.
The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.
Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced a record fall in Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zero deforestation by 2030 and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.
Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.
In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.
So although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:
1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the 59.5% surge of Amazon deforestation under the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.
2 Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.
3 Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.
4 Go on the offensive against US tech giants. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats in Colombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”
5 Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.
6 Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violent gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrations of 2018.
7 Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of the planetary boundaries essential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.
The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”
Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.
