title: Israeli election: Netanyahu, main rival fall short of majority after all votes counted
content_c:
Israel election: Majority remains elusive after final count
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 30, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- The final vote count showed Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc finished with 53 seats
- The anti-Netanyahu bloc, led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, claimed 48 seats
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- As neither party won an outright majority, difficult coalition talks are expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election.
Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins
Ahead of the election, two clear coalitions had formed. On the one side, the ruling coalition of right-wing, far-right and religious parties centered around Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party.
On the other side was the anti-Netanyahu bloc, made up of a coalition of right-wing, centrist and liberal parties whose unifying principle was to oust Netanyahu from power.
However, neither of these blocs was able to secure a majority of seats, meaning a simple path to forming a government is off the table.
The task of figuring out a new working coalition is now beginning, with the question of whether the two Arab-Israeli lists, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats, may form part of a future government or at least provide some form of support.
Yair Golan, chairman of the left-liberal Democrats, said he had met with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid and Mansur Abbas, head of the Arab Ra'am party.
He has called for discussions with the Arab-led parties, saying after his meeting with Eisenkot that "the rescue of Israel is at stake," in a post on X.
It remains to be seen if the right-wing factions of Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc would ultimately entertain the possibility of working with the Arab-led parties.
Another option that has been aired is the possibility of a unity government including both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, but such a move may be similarly distasteful for moderate voters.
Final count released
The final count of ballots from Tuesday's vote has been released by Israel's Central Election Committee.
Netanyahu's bloc with a total of 53 seats
- Likud - 27
- UTJ - 7
- Otzma Yehudit - 7
- Shas - 6
- RZP - 6
Eisenkot's bloc with a total of 48 seats
- Yashar - 21
- B'Yachad - 12
- The Democrats - 8
- Yisrael Beytenu - 7
The Arab Israeli parties with a total of 19 seats
- Joint List - 11
- Ra'am - 8
READ: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.
Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”
A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.
Read more in depth coverage of that story, right here.
Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon
With the final tally of votes in Israel's high-stakes parliamentary elections expected on Thursday evening, we take a look at today's events thus far.
- Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party doubled down on allegations that the election has been stolen by Arab parties.
- Netanyahu said that evidence would be handed to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee.
- Netanyahu also referred to statements about the "involvement of foreign entities that interfered and bribed voters in favor of Arab parties," saying they were "an unprecedented shock."
- Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, said political actors should not "exploit the information" that had yet to be clarified "in order undermine the official results."
- Qatar meanwhile, has denied any involvement in such allegations: "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," it said, adding it is accused of buying off the Arab vote.
- Qatar’s foreign minister spokesman Majed Al Ansari spoke of "accusations made by certain Israeli politicians" and said they had "launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes."
- Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of one of the parties in the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
- The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed any investigation into election interference. He said his party had nothing to do with it.
- Israel's Central Elections Committee poured cold water on vote fraud allegeations saying "there is no basis."
- "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," The Times of Israel quoted acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne as having written in a letter.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end
With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.
That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.
Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.
The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.
Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.
Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.
According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.
This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.
The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.
UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law.
"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.
"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."
Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.
He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW
Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.
"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."
Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.
"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.
Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.
WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock
Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.
Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.
GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.
description: With all the votes counted, the pro-Netanyahu bloc finished ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc. But as neither grouping won a majority, tough coalition talks are ahead. Follow DW.
content:
Israel election: Majority remains elusive after final count
Published October 27, 2026last updated October 30, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
- The final vote count showed Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc finished with 53 seats
- The anti-Netanyahu bloc, led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, claimed 48 seats
- At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
- As neither party won an outright majority, difficult coalition talks are expected in the weeks ahead
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election.
Tricky task of forming a working coalition begins
Ahead of the election, two clear coalitions had formed. On the one side, the ruling coalition of right-wing, far-right and religious parties centered around Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party.
On the other side was the anti-Netanyahu bloc, made up of a coalition of right-wing, centrist and liberal parties whose unifying principle was to oust Netanyahu from power.
However, neither of these blocs was able to secure a majority of seats, meaning a simple path to forming a government is off the table.
The task of figuring out a new working coalition is now beginning, with the question of whether the two Arab-Israeli lists, which together secured an unprecedented 19 seats, may form part of a future government or at least provide some form of support.
Yair Golan, chairman of the left-liberal Democrats, said he had met with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, former Prime Minister Yair Lapid and Mansur Abbas, head of the Arab Ra'am party.
He has called for discussions with the Arab-led parties, saying after his meeting with Eisenkot that "the rescue of Israel is at stake," in a post on X.
It remains to be seen if the right-wing factions of Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc would ultimately entertain the possibility of working with the Arab-led parties.
Another option that has been aired is the possibility of a unity government including both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, but such a move may be similarly distasteful for moderate voters.
Final count released
The final count of ballots from Tuesday's vote has been released by Israel's Central Election Committee.
Netanyahu's bloc with a total of 53 seats
- Likud - 27
- UTJ - 7
- Otzma Yehudit - 7
- Shas - 6
- RZP - 6
Eisenkot's bloc with a total of 48 seats
- Yashar - 21
- B'Yachad - 12
- The Democrats - 8
- Yisrael Beytenu - 7
The Arab Israeli parties with a total of 19 seats
- Joint List - 11
- Ra'am - 8
READ: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.
Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”
A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.
Read more in depth coverage of that story, right here.
Israel elections: Where things stand on Thursday afternoon
With the final tally of votes in Israel's high-stakes parliamentary elections expected on Thursday evening, we take a look at today's events thus far.
- Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party doubled down on allegations that the election has been stolen by Arab parties.
- Netanyahu said that evidence would be handed to police, Shin Bet and the Central Elections Committee.
- Netanyahu also referred to statements about the "involvement of foreign entities that interfered and bribed voters in favor of Arab parties," saying they were "an unprecedented shock."
- Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, said political actors should not "exploit the information" that had yet to be clarified "in order undermine the official results."
- Qatar meanwhile, has denied any involvement in such allegations: "We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," it said, adding it is accused of buying off the Arab vote.
- Qatar’s foreign minister spokesman Majed Al Ansari spoke of "accusations made by certain Israeli politicians" and said they had "launched yet another disinformation campaign aiming to drag Qatar into Israeli political disputes."
- Sami Abu Shehadeh, chair of one of the parties in the Arab-led Joint List, called the claims a new phase of "incitement" against Arab-led groups.
- The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed any investigation into election interference. He said his party had nothing to do with it.
- Israel's Central Elections Committee poured cold water on vote fraud allegeations saying "there is no basis."
- "The Knesset elections were conducted lawfully. The integrity of the elections at polling stations was rigorously safeguarded, and to the best of our knowledge, there is no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity," The Times of Israel quoted acting Central Elections Committee director general Dean Livne as having written in a letter.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot blocs far from majority as count nears its end
With 89.8% of ballots counted, the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, compared with 48 seats for the anti-Netanyahu alliance led by former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, according to the Central Election Committee (CEC) as reported by the Times of Israel.
That leaves both blocs far short of the 61 seats needed for a majority.
The two majority Arab parties seem set to win 19 seats between them, a record tally that beats their previous high of 15 seats.
Netanyahu has ruled out working with the Arab parties to gain a majority, but there have been signs that some parties in Eisenkot's bloc might be open to the idea, though Eisenkot himself has also previously rejected it.
The absentee ballots — "double-envelope" votes — whose count began on Thursday are not expected to materially affect the final results, despite making up almost 10% of the overall vote.
Final tally underway, including 'double envelope' absentee ballots
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) has said that counting of so-called double envelope ballots began early Thursday morning, according to the Times of Israel.
Such ballots are cast mostly by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their assigned polling stations.
According to Israeli media, the CEC is reckoning with between 430,000 and 480,000 such ballots, lower than its previous prediction of some 600,000 but still representing just under 10% of votes cast.
This could theoretically still impact seat distribution to a considerable extent.
The Times of Israel also cited the CEC as saying that not all regular votes have been completely counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by Thursday afternoon, although the official finalized results will not be issued until November 4.
UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'
The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law.
"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.
"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."
Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.
He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.
"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."
'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW
Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.
"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."
Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.
"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.
Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.
WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock
Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.
IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?
A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.
Some small positives may be possible though.
Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.
GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc
Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted
The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.
These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.
This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.
Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.
Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.
A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.
If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.
President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'
President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.
"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."
Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.
"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted
Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra'am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.
Arab list leader calls for Jewish-Arab partnership to oust Netanyahu
The leader of the far-left Joint List, one of Israel's Arab-majority lists, has called for a "genuine Jewish-Arab partnership" to help remove Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"Anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu's blood-soaked government will have to talk to us to secure the path to the change that the public in Israel longs for," Yousef Jabareen told Israeli media.
"We will know how to use our political strength to advance the values we believe in," Jabareen said.
"We are ready to pave the way for the replacement of the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich — and send them home."
After most votes have been counted from Tuesday's election, the conservative Islamist Ra'am party and the Joint List are projected to win a combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
As neither the pro-Netanyahu bloc nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot seem likely to win a majority, the Arab parties could play a key role in the formation of the next government.
Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
However, at least one opposition party is open to the idea, with the leader of the left-leading Democrats, Yair Golan, saying Wednesday he supported bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition.

title: Bosnien und Herzegowina: Militärhubschrauber abgestürzt - vier Tote
content_c:
Bosnien und Herzegowina Vier Tote bei Absturz von Militärhubschrauber
Beim Absturz eines Militärhubschraubers der EU-Friedenstruppe in Bosnien und Herzegowina sind vier Menschen ums Leben gekommen. Die Insassen kamen alle aus Italien. Der genaue Hergang ist noch unklar.
Beim Absturz eines italienischen Militärhubschraubers der EU-Friedenstruppe in Bosnien und Herzegowina sind vier Menschen ums Leben gekommen. Elf weitere Insassen des Helikopters wurden verletzt, wie die EU-Mission (Eufor) am Abend mitteilte.
Nach Angaben der italienischen Regierung in Rom kamen alle Insassen des Hubschraubers aus Italien. Bei den meisten von ihnen handelt es sich um Soldaten. Unter den Todesopfern sind auch zwei Angehörige des Roten Kreuzes.
Der Absturz ereignete sich nach Angaben der EU-Mission am Nachmittag in der Nähe des Dorfes Gorice im Gebiet Brčko an der Grenze zu Kroatien während eines Routineflugs.
Der genaue Hergang ist noch unklar. Bei dem Hubschrauber handelt es sich um einen CH-47 Chinook, einen großen Transporthubschrauber mit zwei Rotoren. Italiens Staatspräsident Sergio Mattarella sprach den Familien der Opfer sein Beileid aus.
EU-Mission seit 2004 in Bosnien im Einsatz
Die EU-Mission überwacht seit 2004 die Umsetzung des Dayton-Friedensabkommens, mit dem 1995 der Bosnien-Krieg beendet wurde - und soll damit für Sicherheit sorgen. Weitere Ziele sind die Ausbildung der bosnischen Streitkräfte und die Schaffung eines sicheren Umfelds für die Entwicklung des Landes.
In Bosnien und Herzegowina gibt es mehr als 30 Jahre nach Kriegsende weiter erhebliche Spannungen zwischen den Volksgruppen der Serben, Kroaten und der bosnischen Muslime. Vor allem auf Seiten der bosnischen Serben bestehen Tendenzen zu einer Abspaltung beziehungsweise einem Anschluss an Serbien.
Aktuell sind mehr als Tausend Soldaten im Einsatz, auch aus Deutschland. Italien leitet seit Beginn des Jahres die Mission. Die italienische Botschafterin in Bosnien und Herzegowina, Sarah Castellani, berichtete im Fernsehsender Tg4, dass sich das Unglück unmittelbar nach dem Start ereignet habe.

title: Israel nach der Wahl: Hoffnung auf eine Regierung ohne Extremisten
content_c:
Israel nach der Wahl: Hoffnung auf eine Regierung ohne Extremisten
29. Oktober 2026
Auch zwei Tage nach der Parlamentswahl in Israel halten sich deutsche Politikerinnen und Politiker mit Bewertungen zurück. Noch ist offen, wer künftig die Regierung führen wird. Zwar liegt das rechts-religiöse Lager des amtierenden Ministerpräsidenten Benjamin Netanjahu vor dem Oppositions-Block des früheren Militärchefs Gadi Eisenkot, aber beide Lager haben keine Mehrheit im Parlament. Eine Regierungsbildung dürfte deshalb extrem schwierig werden.
Der Sprecher von Bundesaußenminister Johann Wadephul (CDU), Martin Giese, vermied am Mittwoch in der Bundespressekonferenz in Berlin eine Bewertung. Zugleich betonte er, Deutschland stehe über Botschafter Alexander Graf Lambsdorff mit allen relevanten Politikern in Israel in Kontakt: "Der jüdische Staat und Deutschland sind durch unsere Geschichte untrennbar miteinander verbunden, und wir werden alles dafür tun, mit jeder zukünftigen Regierung gut zusammenzuarbeiten."
Alabali Radovan: "Der Winter in Gaza wird hart!"
Eine zentrale Sorge der Bundesregierung gilt der Versorgung der Menschen im Gaza-Streifen. Könnten langwierige Koalitionsverhandlungen notwendige Fortschritte verzögern? Entwicklungsministerin Reem Alabali Radovan (SPD) , die gerade den Libanon besucht, warnte gegenüber "Politico": "Der Winter kommt jetzt, der wird hart." Deshalb müsse es mehr Hilfsmöglichkeiten für Hilfsorganisationen in Gaza geben – und das könne nicht auf Koalitionsverhandlungen warten.
Im Gespräch mit der DW und dem Sender RTL fügte sie mit dem Blick auf die palästinensischen Gebiete hinzu: "Die radikale Siedlergewalt muss gestoppt werden. Die Regierung Netanjahu ist weiter geschäftsführend im Amt, und deshalb gilt weiterhin, dass diese Situation beendet werden muss."
Zunehmende Distanz zu Netanjahus Regierung
Die Beziehungen zwischen Deutschland und Israel gelten traditionell als besonders eng – auch aus der historischen Verantwortung Deutschlands für den Mord an Millionen europäischer Juden während der NS-Zeit. Zuletzt ging die Bundesregierung jedoch zunehmend auf Distanz zu Netanjahus Politik, zumindest in ihrer öffentlichen Rhetorik.
Zuletzt hatte Außenminister Johann Wadephul (CDU) nach einer großen israelischen Militäroperation in der Nähe der Stadt Hebron gesagt: "Israel ist völkerrechtlich ganz klar dazu verpflichtet, auch die Rechte der Palästinenserinnen und Palästinenser zu wahren und zu schützen." Bei der Aktion wurden rund 3.000 Palästinenser aus ihren Häusern vertrieben. Zuvor hatten Palästinenser zwei israelische Soldaten ermordet.
In Berlin wird seit Langem darüber spekuliert, ob sich die deutsche Israel-Politik nach der Wahl verändern könnte. Klar ist bislang: Anders als zahlreiche andere, auch europäische Staaten will Deutschland einen palästinensischen Staat vorerst nicht anerkennen. Zugleich hofft Deutschland, dass der künftigen Regierung religiöse, teils rechtsextreme Politiker wie der gegenwärtige Finanzminister Bezalel Smotrich nicht mehr angehören.
CDU hofft auf Regierung aus der Mitte des politischen Spektrums
So sagte der Außenexperte der konservativen CDU im Bundestag, Jürgen Hardt, der DW: "Ich denke, es wäre das Beste für Israel, eine Regierung zu finden, die näher an der Mitte des politischen Spektrums liegt. Das ist natürlich etwas, was die Menschen und vor allem die gewählten Politiker herausfinden müssen. Aber es ist ermutigend, dass so viele Menschen an der Wahl teilgenommen haben. Israel ist eine lebendige Demokratie. Die einzige in der Region, was wir immer betonen sollten."
Große Zuwächse an Stimmen hatten auf jeden Fall Parteien bei der Israel-Wahl, die von arabisch-stämmigen Israelis geführt werden. Sie werden zumeist dem gegenwärtigen Oppositionslager zugerechnet. Dazu sagte der Vize-Präsident des deutschen Bundestags, der Grünen-Politiker Omid-Nouripour, der DW: "Die große Kampagne von Netanjahus Lager in erster Linie gegen die arabischen Israelis hat sehr stark mobilisiert." Wegen der scharfen Kritik des Premiers seien eben viele arabisch-stämmige Israelis überhaupt zur Wahl gegangen. Das, so Nouripour, sei eine gute Nachricht für die Demokratie in Israel.
Jürgen Hardt kann sich auch eine Minderheitsregierung unter Führung von Gadi Eisenkot vorstellen, die von Parteien mit arabischstämmigen Israelis unterstützt wird. Voraussetzung sei allerdings, so der CDU-Politiker, dass diese Gruppierungen jede Form von Terror gegen Israel ablehnten.
description: Deutsche Politiker warten ab: Noch ist unklar, wer Israel künftig regiert. Die Sorge gilt auch Gaza: Welche Folgen hätte ein Machtvakuum? Viele hoffen zudem auf eine Regierung ohne religiöse Hardliner.

Der Sprecher von Bundesaußenminister Johann Wadephul (CDU), Martin Giese, vermied am Mittwoch in der Bundespressekonferenz in Berlin eine Bewertung. Zugleich betonte er, Deutschland stehe über Botschafter Alexander Graf Lambsdorff mit allen relevanten Politikern in Israel in Kontakt: "Der jüdische Staat und Deutschland sind durch unsere Geschichte untrennbar miteinander verbunden, und wir werden alles dafür tun, mit jeder zukünftigen Regierung gut zusammenzuarbeiten."
Alabali Radovan: "Der Winter in Gaza wird hart!"
Eine zentrale Sorge der Bundesregierung gilt der Versorgung der Menschen im Gaza-Streifen. Könnten langwierige Koalitionsverhandlungen notwendige Fortschritte verzögern? Entwicklungsministerin Reem Alabali Radovan (SPD) , die gerade den Libanon besucht, warnte gegenüber "Politico": "Der Winter kommt jetzt, der wird hart." Deshalb müsse es mehr Hilfsmöglichkeiten für Hilfsorganisationen in Gaza geben – und das könne nicht auf Koalitionsverhandlungen warten.
Im Gespräch mit der DW und dem Sender RTL fügte sie mit dem Blick auf die palästinensischen Gebiete hinzu: "Die radikale Siedlergewalt muss gestoppt werden. Die Regierung Netanjahu ist weiter geschäftsführend im Amt, und deshalb gilt weiterhin, dass diese Situation beendet werden muss."
Zunehmende Distanz zu Netanjahus Regierung
Die Beziehungen zwischen Deutschland und Israel gelten traditionell als besonders eng – auch aus der historischen Verantwortung Deutschlands für den Mord an Millionen europäischer Juden während der NS-Zeit. Zuletzt ging die Bundesregierung jedoch zunehmend auf Distanz zu Netanjahus Politik, zumindest in ihrer öffentlichen Rhetorik.
Zuletzt hatte Außenminister Johann Wadephul (CDU) nach einer großen israelischen Militäroperation in der Nähe der Stadt Hebron gesagt: "Israel ist völkerrechtlich ganz klar dazu verpflichtet, auch die Rechte der Palästinenserinnen und Palästinenser zu wahren und zu schützen." Bei der Aktion wurden rund 3.000 Palästinenser aus ihren Häusern vertrieben. Zuvor hatten Palästinenser zwei israelische Soldaten ermordet.
In Berlin wird seit Langem darüber spekuliert, ob sich die deutsche Israel-Politik nach der Wahl verändern könnte. Klar ist bislang: Anders als zahlreiche andere, auch europäische Staaten will Deutschland einen palästinensischen Staat vorerst nicht anerkennen. Zugleich hofft Deutschland, dass der künftigen Regierung religiöse, teils rechtsextreme Politiker wie der gegenwärtige Finanzminister Bezalel Smotrich nicht mehr angehören.
CDU hofft auf Regierung aus der Mitte des politischen Spektrums
So sagte der Außenexperte der konservativen CDU im Bundestag, Jürgen Hardt, der DW: "Ich denke, es wäre das Beste für Israel, eine Regierung zu finden, die näher an der Mitte des politischen Spektrums liegt. Das ist natürlich etwas, was die Menschen und vor allem die gewählten Politiker herausfinden müssen. Aber es ist ermutigend, dass so viele Menschen an der Wahl teilgenommen haben. Israel ist eine lebendige Demokratie. Die einzige in der Region, was wir immer betonen sollten."
Große Zuwächse an Stimmen hatten auf jeden Fall Parteien bei der Israel-Wahl, die von arabisch-stämmigen Israelis geführt werden. Sie werden zumeist dem gegenwärtigen Oppositionslager zugerechnet. Dazu sagte der Vize-Präsident des deutschen Bundestags, der Grünen-Politiker Omid-Nouripour, der DW: "Die große Kampagne von Netanjahus Lager in erster Linie gegen die arabischen Israelis hat sehr stark mobilisiert." Wegen der scharfen Kritik des Premiers seien eben viele arabisch-stämmige Israelis überhaupt zur Wahl gegangen. Das, so Nouripour, sei eine gute Nachricht für die Demokratie in Israel.
Jürgen Hardt kann sich auch eine Minderheitsregierung unter Führung von Gadi Eisenkot vorstellen, die von Parteien mit arabischstämmigen Israelis unterstützt wird. Voraussetzung sei allerdings, so der CDU-Politiker, dass diese Gruppierungen jede Form von Terror gegen Israel ablehnten.

title: Великий обласний центр накрив блекаут: зупинився увесь електротранспорт — влада звернулась до людей
content_c:
Великий обласний центр накрив блекаут: зупинився електротранспорт — влада звернулась до людей (оновлено)
Після нічної атаки на Дніпро у місті виник масштабний блекаут. Енергетики працювали до самого ранку, але навантаження на систему дуже велике. Основні системи життєзабезпечення міста перейшли на роботу від генераторів.
Що відомо про відключення світла в обласному центрі — читайте на сайті ТСН.ua.
Вночі місцева влада повідомила, що через обстріл без електропостачання залишилися понад 350 тис. абонентів у Дніпр та навколишніх населених пунктах. Насосні станції водопостачання ті водовідведення перевели на резервне живлення від генераторів.
Блекаут у Дніпрі — що відомо
Зранку очільник Дніпропетровської ОВА Олександр Ганжа повідомив, що енергетики повернули світло частині споживачів Дніпропетровщини. Втім, виявилося, що енергосистема не витримує навантаження, — Дніпро знову знеструмлений.
«Енергосистема, пошкоджена ворожими ударами, не витримує навантаження. Відновлювальні роботи тривають і зараз. Основні системи життєзабезпечення міста переходять на роботу від генераторів», — повідомив чиновник.
Рух транспорту
Водночас міський голова Борис Філатов закликає містян сьогодні залишитися вдома, адже Дніпро може охопити транспортний колапс. У місті не працює електротранспорт.
«Будь ласка, якщо є можливість, залишайтесь вдома. Окрім автобусів, жоден електротранспорт не працює: ані трамваї, ані тролейбуси, ані метро», — наголосив мер.
В офіційному Телеграм-каналі Департаменту транспортної інфраструктури «Транспорт Дніпра» повідомили, що частково відновлено живлення метрополітену.
«Рух поїздів виконується за графіком вихідного дня. Інтервал руху поїздів складає 16 хв», — йдеться у повідомленні.
Екстрені відключення
Зранку у ДТЕК повідомили, що на Дніпропетровщині запровадили екстрені відключення світла. Графіки не діють у Дніпрі, прилеглих районах до обласного центру і у частині Павлоградського району.
«В області серйозно пошкоджено обладнання через атаки ворога. Енергетики працюють, щоб якомога швидше заживити об’єкти критичної інфраструктури та повернути світло до осель», — йдеться у повідомленні.

title: Россия атаковала баллистикой промышленное предприятие в Кременчуге
content_c:
Ночью 30 октября россияне нанесли удар по Полтавской области с помощью баллистических ракет. Под ударом врага оказалось одно из промышленных предприятий, сообщил глава областной военной администрации Виталий Дякивнич.
«В Кременчугском районе враг атаковал одно из промышленных предприятий. Информация уточняется», — говорится в сообщении.
Очередную за ночь ракетную угрозу объявили в 2:59. Через несколько минут после этого Воздушные силы и мониторинговые каналы сообщили о запуске ракет в направлении Кременчуга. По данным мониторинговых каналов, по Кременчугу, а также Светловодску Кировоградской области враг выпустил девять «Цирконов»/КР-23.
Отметим, что поздно вечером 29 октября россияне также нанесли баллистический удар по Киеву, в результате чего погиб человек. В Дарницком районе произошло попадание в складские здания. Возник пожар. В Днепровском районе горят обломки ракеты во дворе одного из жилых комплексов. Впоследствии стало известно, что речь идет о ЖК «Комфорт Таун». Там взрывная волна выбила окна в домах, повредила цветочный магазин и кафе на первых этажах, а также многоуровневую парковку на территории ЖК.

title: "Жодного порушення". В Олешках вже дві доби тримається режим тиші, готують евакуацію
content_c:
"Жодного порушення". В Олешках вже дві доби тримається режим тиші, готують евакуацію
  - Author, Відділ новин
  - Role, BBC News Україна
- Published
- Час прочитання: 4 хв
Режим тиші в окупованому російськими військами місті Олешки вже понад дві доби триває без порушень. Про це повідомили український омбудсмен Дмитро Лубінець та уповноважена з прав людини в Росії Яна Лантратова.
"Сторони повністю виконують взяті на себе зобов'язання, жодного порушення не зафіксовано", — написала у соцмережах Лантратова.
Дмитро Лубінець зазначив, що режим тиші вдається підтримувати, зокрема завдяки "постійній комунікації" між уповноваженими з прав людини в Росії та Україні.
"Ми перебуваємо на зв'язку і координуємо виконання досягнутих домовленостей", — наголосив Лубінець.
Яна Лантратова повідомила, що для жителів Олешок сформували велику гуманітарну колону з продуктами, медикаментами та всім необхідним.
За словами Лубінця, гуманітарну допомогу для жителів міста доставлять в п'ятницю, 30 жовтня.
"Продовжуємо працювати над виконанням домовленостей. Наше завдання — доставити гуманітарну допомогу людям, які залишаються в місті, та забезпечити можливість безпечного виїзду цивільних", — зазначив Дмитро Лубінець.
Розмінування доріг і підготовка до евакуації
Наразі триває розмінування маршрутів, необхідних для проведення гуманітарної місії, розповів Дмитро Лубінець.
Міністерство оборони Росії повідомило, що військовослужбовці угруповання військ "Дніпро" розміновують дороги, прилеглі до Олешок, для доставки допомоги та організації евакуації жителів.
У Кремлі розраховують, що гуманітарну допомогу доставлять не пізніше 30 жовтня, а всі охочі зможуть залишити місто, заявив прессекретар президента РФ Дмитро Пєсков.
"Ми знаємо, що вже вилетів борт із Москви. Там буде досить складна схема, як вони діставатимуться", — сказав він в інтерв'ю російському виданню "Известия".
Українська делегація на чолі з Дмитром Лубінцем через Білорусь вирушила в бік Олешок. Жителі міста, які захочуть евакуюватися в Україну, за планом 31 жовтня разом з українською делегацією вилетять з російського міста Анапа до білоруського Гомеля, а потім — до України.
Білоруське агентство БЕЛТА опублікувало фотографії прибуття української делегації на чолі з Лубінцем до Гомеля, підкресливши, що це "перша очна зустріч російської та української делегацій, які беруть участь у гуманітарній операції на херсонському напрямку".
З Гомеля, як зазначає білоруське державне агентство, делегації вилетіли одним літаком.
Раніше телеканал Fox News повідомив, що жителів міста Олешки Херсонської області, які вирішать евакуюватися в Україну, вивозитимуть до Білорусі літаком Міністерства оборони Росії.
Телеканал також повідомляв, що супроводжуватиме жителів Олешок українська делегація на чолі з омбудсменом Дмитром Лубінцем.
Хто їде в Олешки від США
У своїй заяві на сайті Білого дому Меланія Трамп зазначала, що у складі гуманітарної місії до Олешок поїде американське медіа. Вони мають висвітлювати, як людей рятують.
Пізніше у Х перша леді США уточнила, що це будуть чотири американські журналісти з телеканалу Newsmax.
"Виступаючи нейтральними спостерігачами, вони незалежно висвітлюватимуть і документуватимуть цю історичну гуманітарну місію, створюючи її постійний документальний запис", - заявила Меланія.
“Наскільки розумію, на цю мить офіційні представники США не планують брати участі в евакуації на місці”, - розповідає колишній журналіст "Голосу Америки", медіарадник фонду "Razom for Ukraine" в США Остап Яриш.
За даними Яриша, людина, яка від США відповідає за план евакуації з Олешок - Марк Бекман, приватний консультант, а також продюсер фільму про першу леді США "Меланія".
"Попри хибні уявлення, він не є посадовцем США і не працює в офісі Першої Леді (у соцмережах вказує свою роль як "ексклюзивний старший радник"). З Меланією Трамп Бекмана пов'язує багаторічна співпраця над її медійними та бізнес-проєктами, зокрема над документальною стрічкою", - розповідає Яриш.
Спецпредставник президента РФ Кирило Дмитрієв у четвер 29 жовтня привітав представників телеканалу Newsmax у Росії.
Режим тиші за посередництва Меланії Трамп і Папи Римського
В Олешках Херсонської області, що перебувають під російським контролем, протягом останніх кількох місяців склалася ситуація, близька до гуманітарної катастрофи.
Місто перебувало під постійними обстрілами, а залишити його було практично неможливо, оскільки більшість доріг заміновані. У місті майже немає світла, не працює водопостачання, а останній продуктовий магазин закрився ще взимку.
У місті на лівому березі Дніпра, де до початку російського вторгнення в Україну проживали 24 тисячі людей, зараз залишається приблизно півтори тисячі осіб, зокрема близько 40 дітей.
Переважно це літні та маломобільні люди з тяжкими захворюваннями, а також люди без документів.

content:
"Жодного порушення". В Олешках вже дві доби тримається режим тиші, готують евакуацію
  - Author, Відділ новин
  - Role, BBC News Україна
- Published
- Час прочитання: 4 хв
Режим тиші в окупованому російськими військами місті Олешки вже понад дві доби триває без порушень. Про це повідомили український омбудсмен Дмитро Лубінець та уповноважена з прав людини в Росії Яна Лантратова.
"Сторони повністю виконують взяті на себе зобов'язання, жодного порушення не зафіксовано", — написала у соцмережах Лантратова.
Дмитро Лубінець зазначив, що режим тиші вдається підтримувати, зокрема завдяки "постійній комунікації" між уповноваженими з прав людини в Росії та Україні.
"Ми перебуваємо на зв'язку і координуємо виконання досягнутих домовленостей", — наголосив Лубінець.
Яна Лантратова повідомила, що для жителів Олешок сформували велику гуманітарну колону з продуктами, медикаментами та всім необхідним.
За словами Лубінця, гуманітарну допомогу для жителів міста доставлять в п'ятницю, 30 жовтня.
"Продовжуємо працювати над виконанням домовленостей. Наше завдання — доставити гуманітарну допомогу людям, які залишаються в місті, та забезпечити можливість безпечного виїзду цивільних", — зазначив Дмитро Лубінець.
Розмінування доріг і підготовка до евакуації
Наразі триває розмінування маршрутів, необхідних для проведення гуманітарної місії, розповів Дмитро Лубінець.
Міністерство оборони Росії повідомило, що військовослужбовці угруповання військ "Дніпро" розміновують дороги, прилеглі до Олешок, для доставки допомоги та організації евакуації жителів.
У Кремлі розраховують, що гуманітарну допомогу доставлять не пізніше 30 жовтня, а всі охочі зможуть залишити місто, заявив прессекретар президента РФ Дмитро Пєсков.
"Ми знаємо, що вже вилетів борт із Москви. Там буде досить складна схема, як вони діставатимуться", — сказав він в інтерв'ю російському виданню "Известия".
Українська делегація на чолі з Дмитром Лубінцем через Білорусь вирушила в бік Олешок. Жителі міста, які захочуть евакуюватися в Україну, за планом 31 жовтня разом з українською делегацією вилетять з російського міста Анапа до білоруського Гомеля, а потім — до України.
Білоруське агентство БЕЛТА опублікувало фотографії прибуття української делегації на чолі з Лубінцем до Гомеля, підкресливши, що це "перша очна зустріч російської та української делегацій, які беруть участь у гуманітарній операції на херсонському напрямку".
З Гомеля, як зазначає білоруське державне агентство, делегації вилетіли одним літаком.
Раніше телеканал Fox News повідомив, що жителів міста Олешки Херсонської області, які вирішать евакуюватися в Україну, вивозитимуть до Білорусі літаком Міністерства оборони Росії.
Телеканал також повідомляв, що супроводжуватиме жителів Олешок українська делегація на чолі з омбудсменом Дмитром Лубінцем.
Хто їде в Олешки від США
У своїй заяві на сайті Білого дому Меланія Трамп зазначала, що у складі гуманітарної місії до Олешок поїде американське медіа. Вони мають висвітлювати, як людей рятують.
Пізніше у Х перша леді США уточнила, що це будуть чотири американські журналісти з телеканалу Newsmax.
"Виступаючи нейтральними спостерігачами, вони незалежно висвітлюватимуть і документуватимуть цю історичну гуманітарну місію, створюючи її постійний документальний запис", - заявила Меланія.
“Наскільки розумію, на цю мить офіційні представники США не планують брати участі в евакуації на місці”, - розповідає колишній журналіст "Голосу Америки", медіарадник фонду "Razom for Ukraine" в США Остап Яриш.
За даними Яриша, людина, яка від США відповідає за план евакуації з Олешок - Марк Бекман, приватний консультант, а також продюсер фільму про першу леді США "Меланія".
"Попри хибні уявлення, він не є посадовцем США і не працює в офісі Першої Леді (у соцмережах вказує свою роль як "ексклюзивний старший радник"). З Меланією Трамп Бекмана пов'язує багаторічна співпраця над її медійними та бізнес-проєктами, зокрема над документальною стрічкою", - розповідає Яриш.
Спецпредставник президента РФ Кирило Дмитрієв у четвер 29 жовтня привітав представників телеканалу Newsmax у Росії.
Режим тиші за посередництва Меланії Трамп і Папи Римського
В Олешках Херсонської області, що перебувають під російським контролем, протягом останніх кількох місяців склалася ситуація, близька до гуманітарної катастрофи.
Місто перебувало під постійними обстрілами, а залишити його було практично неможливо, оскільки більшість доріг заміновані. У місті майже немає світла, не працює водопостачання, а останній продуктовий магазин закрився ще взимку.

title: Кількість постраждалих у Чернігові зросла до 35 осіб включно з чотирма дітьми – міськрада
content_c:
Кількість постраждалих унаслідок російської атаки на Чернігів зросла до 35 осіб, серед яких четверо дітей, вісьмох поранених госпіталізували, повідомила пресслужба Чернігівської міської ради у четвер ввечері.
"Кількість постраждалих зросла до 35 осіб, серед них – 4 дітей. Госпіталізовано 8 осіб, з них 3 дітей", – ідеться в повідомленні міськради у телеграм-каналі.
За даними відомства, у медичних закладах міста на стаціонарному лікуванні наразі перебувають п'ятеро дорослих і троє неповнолітніх, які зазнали поранень під час ворожого обстрілу.
Як повідомлялося, внаслідок удару російського БпЛА по Чернігову 29 жовтня загинули двоє 15-річних дівчат, серед постраждалих діти, зокрема 10-місячна дівчинка.
П'ятниця, 30 жовтня, оголошена в місті Днем жалоби за жителями, які загинули внаслідок російських ударів у період із 21 до 29 жовтня.

title: 'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
content_c:
'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
- Published
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
content_c:
Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
- Published
Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.
Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.
Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.
The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.
The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.
Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.
Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.
Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.
According to the latest figures up to 30 September, external, 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.
The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.
However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.
- Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says

She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system.

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
content_c:
DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
- Published
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.
DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.
Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.
"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.
"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.
For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.
He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".
The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.
Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.
"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.
In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.
DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.
The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.
New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."
"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

title: El Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea a ‘national crisis’ as rivers dry up and local farms fail
content_c:
Extreme drought driven by an historic El Niño is affecting as many as 8 million people in Papua New Guinea, causing a cascade of issues from shortages of food and water, to electricity scarcity and schooling disruption.
An influential coalition that includes churches, trade unions and business groups has said the Pacific nation is in the midst of a “national crisis”, but there appears to be “no coordinated plan to protect vulnerable communities from the worsening impacts of El Niño.”
Residents and community leaders have told the Guardian that rivers and creeks have dried up and family food gardens – a vital source of food and income for many – have shrivelled. Schools and health facilities are being forced to close early because they lack sufficient water to provide basic services.
Emilly Meren, humanitarian projects manager at CARE International in PNG, said in rural highland areas families were rationing food to one meal a day – while food insecurity was leading to localised disputes between families.
“For women and girls, they are expected to do more to support their families,” she said, yet they were “the last to eat because they have to serve others first”.
“They have to travel three to four hours to source water and food and are exposed to a heightened risk of harassment. We are hearing stories of transactional sex happening in the community – exchanging sex for money or for food.”
The El Niño climate pattern is gaining strength in the tropical Pacific with forecasts suggesting it will be the strongest ever recorded with its impacts worsened by global heating.
Some parts of PNG have had less than a quarter of their usual rainfall since August.
The PNG National Weather Service declared the onset of El Niño in June but Kasis Inape, the service’s assistant director, said at that point, much of the country was already in drought and about 8 million people had been affected.
Inape said PNG was one of the wettest places in the world with rain fed by warm tropical waters, but the El Niño had seen those waters shift east “and we’re starved of rain”.
“Because we’re a rain-fed country, a lot of our people are subsistence farmers and they depend just on rainfall to survive and to feed themselves,” he said.
PNG’s wet season is between November and April and Inape said while some short term relief was forecasted, there were concerns El Niño would shorten the season.
“The place is so dry – just two months of rain is not enough to allow crops to grow and water levels to be comfortable,” Inape said.
In Morobe province’s Bulolo district, smaller rivers have dried up leaving families without access to water for drinking, cooking and washing.
Resident Theophil Zarack said many schools and health centres were operating for only half a day, with some clinics no longer accepting inpatients due to a lack of available water.
Martha Zureno, a resident in Leklu village, said: “All our rivers have dried up, including the one behind my house. Now, my children and I have to walk for miles every afternoon to fetch water for cooking and drinking from the other side.
“We have a well that we dug ourselves, but we only use that water for washing. All the crops in our gardens have dried up and died, and we cannot grow anything now.”
Zureno said that most of the local residents depend on panning for gold to earn an income, but without water, “even that has become increasingly difficult”.
Meanwhile, a destructive hailstorm in parts of Enga province earlier this month – not blamed directly on El Niño – buried sweet potatoes under ice, exacerbating the food scarcity issue, according to George Iki, president of the Sambe Unity Development Association.
In the capital Port Moresby, PNG Power has begun planned electricity blackouts after falling dam levels cut hydropower generation and said disruptions could continue for up to 10 months. The company was working to manage dam releases to protect the city’s water supply.
Peter Aitsi, a prominent PNG business figure and co-chair of the Community Coalition Against Corruption, said the government needed to carry out “proper assessments” of the unfurling impacts, particularly on rural communities.
Last month the group called the drought situation a “national crisis”, but according to Aitsi, urban centres have been mostly shielded from the impacts. That could change, however, with electricity blackouts and a shortage of fresh food from drought-stricken areas, he said.
Aitsi said the capital had been covered in a smoke haze in the past week from fires elsewhere on the island, and in Indonesia to the west, that scientists say have been fuelled by El Niño.
Prime minister James Marape has directed provincial and district authorities to prepare for a prolonged dry season, saying his government was examining financial arrangements to support disaster responses.
“Cabinet is looking at tailoring provisions of our financial instructions to make sure that districts and provinces are assisted to respond to disasters as they happen where appropriate,” Marape said.

title: HMRC puts 200 billionaires on UK tax crackdown hitlist
content_c:
The UK’s tax authority is assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires as part of a crackdown meant to raise £500m for the public purse.
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) said it had for the first time compiled a list of billionaires who are required to pay tax in the UK, regardless of whether they formally live in the country, to tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they ought.
In an announcement after Wednesday’s budget, the authority said it was allocating a customer compliance manager (CCM) to each billionaire with a UK tax footprint, whose complex tax affairs are often hard for HMRC to manage.
“Billionaires can present a particular example of this, with affairs often spanning multiple taxes, entities and jurisdictions and a greater need for early and coordinated engagement,” HMRC said.
It said the managers would offer voluntary discussions to each billionaire before they filed their taxes, to “help build a shared understanding of the customers’ UK tax affairs and make subsequent engagement more focused and proportionate”.
The authority also plans to start deploying new tech to monitor wealthy individuals – defined as those with income of more than £200,000 or assets over £2m in any of the last three years – involving “advanced analytics, automated triggers and artificial intelligence (AI) to identify emerging risks earlier and target compliance activity where it will have greatest impact”.
It is part of wider efforts to tackle the wealthy tax gap, whereby rich people are failing to pay what they should if all of their assets were disclosed to the tax authority. The wealthy tax gap for 2024-25 was estimated to be worth £3.6bn, equivalent to 6% of the total tax gap across the UK’s entire tax-paying population.
The tax authority said its actions would contribute at least £500m towards a larger commitment to raise £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.
HMRC was grilled in July last year by MPs on the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.
 
 
 Adam Craggs, the head of tax, investigations and financial crime at the law firm RPC, said anyone with more than £200,000 of annual income, or net assets above £2m, should now “reflect on how clearly they understand and can evidence their UK tax position and their interaction with HMRC”.

title: Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
content_c:
Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
October 29, 2026
German tennis star Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in tennis, capping a successful year where he won two Grand Slams.
Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.
Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.
Zverev got there by reaching the quarter-finals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.
He is also the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe.
"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.
"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."
Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.
Two Grand Slams in 2026
Zverev's career had been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching them, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.
The Hamburg-born also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.
But his tennis career finally had its breakthrough this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.
Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

title: Elif Eralp: Grünen-Chefin Brantner zeigt Verständnis – Unionsfraktionschef Frei für Abbruch der Koalitionsverhandlungen
content_c:
Aussagen von Elif Eralp Grünen-Chefin zeigt Verständnis für Eralp – Unionsfraktionschef fordert Abbruch der Koalitionsverhandlungen
Nach dem SPIEGEL-Bericht über die Berliner Linken-Spitzenkandidatin Elif Eralp und deren Angst vor Hamas-Sympathisanten hat Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei (CDU) Grüne und SPD zum Abbruch der Koalitionsverhandlungen mit der Linkspartei aufgerufen.
»Wer in den eigenen Reihen die Zusammenarbeit mit Hamas-Sympathisanten duldet, kann nicht glaubwürdig Verantwortung für die Sicherheit von Millionen Berlinern übernehmen«, sagte Frei dem »Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger«. »SPD und Grüne müssen die Notbremse ziehen: Mit dieser Berliner Linken darf es keine Regierungskoalition geben«, forderte er.
Zuvor war bekannt geworden, dass Eralp, die Regierende Bürgermeisterin von Berlin werden will, die Sicherheit ihrer Familie in Gefahr sieht, wenn sie sich explizit zu einem bekannten Palästina-Aktivisten äußert . Ihre Aussagen stammen einem internen Vermerk Eralps, wonach ihr Ehemann und sie »Angst vor diesen Leuten« hätten. Die Äußerung bezog sich auf den Hamas-Sympathisanten Ibrahim Ibrahim.
»Niemand darf Angst um sich und seine Familie haben müssen, das gilt selbstverständlich auch für Frau Eralp«, sagte Frei zu den Vorgängen. »Umso erschütternder ist, dass Teile ihrer eigenen Partei mit genau jenem extremistischen Milieu gemeinsame Sache machen, vor dem sie sich fürchtet.«
Die Bundesvorsitzende der Grünen, Franziska Brantner, äußerte Verständnis für Eralps Aussagen. »Ich finde es sehr nachvollziehbar, dass Elif Eralp Angst hat«, sagte sie dem »»Kölner Stadt-Anzeigers«». Wer von Extremisten und Organisierter Kriminalität bedroht wird, brauche unser Mitgefühl und müsse vor allem geschützt werden.
Der entschlossene Kampf gegen diese Milieus müsse ganz oben auf der Agenda jeder neuen Landesregierung stehen, so die Grünen-Politikerin. »Wer hier glaubwürdig handeln will, muss auch dann konsequent sein, wenn die entsprechenden Strukturen bis in die eigene Partei hineinreichen.«

title: Trauer um britischen Schauspieler: Patrick Stewart gestorben
content_c:
Trauer um britischen Schauspieler Hollywood-Star Patrick Stewart gestorben
Seine Rollen als Captain Picard in Star Trek und Professor Charles Xavier bei X-Men machten ihn weltberühmt. Nun ist der britische Schauspieler Patrick Stewart im Alter von 86 Jahren gestorben.
Der britische Schauspieler Patrick Stewart ist tot. Er starb im Alter von 86 Jahren nach einer Alzheimer-Erkrankung in Los Angeles, wie seine Sprecherin mitteilte. "Er wurde in der warmen Umarmung von Familie und Freunden gehalten, umgeben von Live-Musik, Gebet, Tränen, Lachen und der Art von tiefer Emotion, wie nur er sie nach ein Leben langem Engagement für uns alle inspirieren konnte", hieß es in der Mitteilung. "Seine sonore Stimme und sein einzigartiges Talent werden für immer synonym mit unvergesslichen Darbietungen in jedem Genre sein."
Vor allem spielte Stewart Theater
Stewart wurde 1940 in Mirfield im Norden Englands geboren. Er spielte schon als Jugendlicher in Theatergruppen, bevor er an die Schauspielschule nach Bristol ging. Stewart wandte sich vor allem klassischen Rollen zu und wurde 1966 Mitglied der Royal Shakespeare Company, der er lange Jahre treu blieb.
Er verbrachte den größten Teil seiner Karriere auf der Theaterbühne, spielte Claudius und Macbeth, präsentierte eine Ein-Mann-Darbietung von "A Christmas Carol" und trat zusammen mit seinem Freund Ian McKellen - der auch in "X-Men" seinen Freund und Widersacher Magneto spielte - in Harold Pinters "No Man’s Land" sowie Samuel Becketts "Warten auf Godot" auf.
Die größten Rollen: Picard und Professor X
Ab den 1970er-Jahren spielte Stewart auch in britischen Fernsehfilmen und -Serien mit, unter anderem ist er im beliebten Weihnachtsfilm "Der kleine Lord" als Butler zu sehen.
1987 wurde er für die Rolle des Raumschiff-Kommandeurs Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation" gecastet - die Rolle machte ihn weltberühmt. Als Professor Charles Xavier spielte er in den vergangenen Jahren in zahlreichen "X-Men" und Marvel-Filmen mit.
Stewart war für mehrere Emmys und Golden Globes nominiert. Seit 1996 befindet sich ein Stern mit seinem Namen auf dem Hollywood Walk of Fame. 2009 wurde er von Königin Elizabeth II. zum Knight Bachelor ernannt und durfte sich seither Sir Patrick Stewart nennen.
